battles.why: Houston traded up for a first-round guard and immediately put him on first-team center reps in the spring despite him never having snapped in a real game; Andrews started all 17 in 2025 but was a weak link.
battles.stakes: Determines whether the interior OL that undermined C.J. Stroud in 2025 is actually fixed, and whether Houston's first-round pick plays his natural position or a learned one.
battles.moneyNote: Rutledge was the No. 26 overall pick (Houston traded up two spots) on a four-year, $19.276M fully guaranteed rookie deal. That capital means Rutledge starts *somewhere* almost regardless of camp; what is genuinely open is whether it's center or guard. Andrews is cheap depth with no guarantees protecting him.

battles.why: Teller was acquired to start but is a career right guard being asked to flip sides for the first time since his rookie year; Ingram is locked in at RG on a new extension, so the only interior slot in play is left.
battles.stakes: The left side in front of Stroud's blind side, paired with second-year LT Aireontae Ersery.
battles.moneyNote: Teller is a former All-Pro Houston traded for this offseason and Ingram signed an extension before the draft — both are paid to start. Teams do not trade for and pay a two-time All-Pro guard to lose a camp battle. The realistic outcome is Teller at LG and Rutledge sorted into C or a swing role.

battles.why: Dell has not practiced in roughly 18 months since his 2024 leg injury and missed all of 2025, leaving the third receiver job behind Nico Collins and Jayden Higgins genuinely unclaimed.
battles.stakes: Who gets the volume in three-receiver sets in an offense that has to prove 2025's passing-game collapse was situational.
battles.moneyNote: Noel is a 2025 third-round pick and Higgins a 2025 second-rounder, so the future capital sits with the sophomores. Dell's rookie deal carries no meaningful guarantee leverage, and he has already been floated externally as a trade candidate — his contract will not save the job for him.

battles.why: Danielle Hunter, Will Anderson Jr. and Dylan Horton are locks; the fourth edge spot vacated by Derek Barnett's rotational snaps has no established occupant.
battles.stakes: Roughly 200-250 rotational pass-rush snaps on a defense whose identity is the front four.
battles.moneyNote: Neither player has draft capital or guaranteed money protecting him — Robinson is a low-cost veteran addition with a career high of 1.5 sacks, Byrd a 2024 seventh-rounder. This is one of the few Texans jobs where the depth chart is genuinely blank.

battles.why: Tommy Townsend is gone and Houston brought in two young legs with nothing settled between them.
battles.stakes: Field position for a team built around defense and expected to play low-scoring games.
battles.moneyNote: Houston sent a Day 3 pick swap to acquire Kroeger, which is a thumb on the scale but nowhere near enough capital to decide a specialist job. Stonehouse (undrafted, Syracuse) out-averaged Kroeger's NFL rookie season in college. Genuinely a coin flip.

HOU.biggestUnknown: Whether Keylan Rutledge can actually play center in the NFL. He took 98.3% of his college snaps at right guard, and the entire interior configuration — center, left guard, and where Wyatt Teller ends up — cascades off that one question. Houston has now rebuilt this line in three straight offseasons without solving it.
HOU.campOpens: Veterans and rookies report Tuesday, July 28, 2026; first practice Wednesday, July 29, at the Houston Methodist Training Center. Eight practices are free and open to fans (Aug 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 18).
HOU.notes:
Things a data-driven writer should know:

1. THE MEDIA-MANUFACTURED ONE I DELIBERATELY LEFT OFF: "RB1 competition." Houston traded for David Montgomery to replace Joe Mixon, and the running backs coach has already publicly defined Woody Marks's role as "third downs, special teams" — plus Marks is slotted as the primary kick returner. That is a coach telling you the depth chart in July. Any "Marks vs. Montgomery" framing you see is content, not competition. Nick Chubb and Mixon are not in the 2026 plan.

2. CB3/nickel (Jaylin Smith vs. Tremon Smith) is real enough to mention but I'd grade it likely-settled: Jaylin Smith is a 2025 third-rounder, is reported healthy with no restrictions after the torn meniscus that ended his rookie year, and the staff has publicly praised his pre-injury tape. Tremon Smith is 30 and was the emergency answer. Draft capital plus "we really like his upside" quotes is how these end.

3. Tight end behind Dalton Schultz is the battle I could not report responsibly. Multiple outlets describe four credible candidates for TE2/TE3 snaps and float Houston carrying five tight ends into Week 1, but I could not confirm the individual names from primary reporting and will not invent them. Worth one search of your own — it's a real one.

4. THE STRUCTURAL POINT FOR A DATA PIECE: Houston has spent a first-round pick, a trade for a former All-Pro, a guard extension, a free-agent tackle signing, and a 2025 second-round tackle on the offensive line across two offseasons. Almost every "battle" on this roster is an OL battle. That is the story — not five separate competitions, but one unsolved unit being re-shuffled in public for the third consecutive summer. The rest of the roster (Stroud, Collins, Stingley, Lassiter, Hunter, Anderson, the Blankenship/Bullock safety pairing) is about as settled as any contender's in the league.

5. Caveat on sourcing: WebFetch returned HTTP 403 on ESPN, NFL.com, Yahoo, SI/onSI and Battle Red Blog, so every claim here comes from search-result summarization of those articles rather than full-text reads. The camp date, Rutledge's contract figure, and the Rutledge/Andrews center framing are corroborated across three or more independent outlets and I'd treat those as solid. The punter and DE4 details come from fewer sources — verify before publishing names.

ATL.campOpens: Rookies reported Friday, July 24; veterans report Tuesday, July 28; first full-squad practice Wednesday, July 29 at the team facility in Flowery Branch, GA (camp runs through Aug. 26; 12 open practices July 31–Aug. 20)

battles.why: An entirely new football operation — HC Kevin Stefanski, GM Ian Cunningham, team president Matt Ryan — has no institutional attachment to Penix, who is rehabbing a torn ACL, and it added Tagovailoa in March on a throwaway contract.
battles.stakes: Decides whether 2026 is a bridge/evaluation year or the season Penix's No. 8 overall selection is validated, and it sets up the franchise's 2027 QB decision.
battles.moneyNote: Tagovailoa signed a one-year deal worth roughly $1.3M — essentially the minimum — because Miami still owes him $54M guaranteed for 2026 after releasing him, so Atlanta carries no financial obligation to play him. Penix's leverage is draft capital (No. 8 overall, 2024) held by a previous regime, which is the weakest form of protection there is. Neither man is protected by money, which is exactly why this one is real. Health, not merit, may settle it: reporting has Tagovailoa favored for Week 1 mainly because Penix is still working back from ACL surgery.

battles.why: Atlanta has been among the league's worst slot-coverage teams two years running and responded by stacking the room with low-cost veterans, returnees and young fliers rather than a clear answer.
battles.stakes: The slot is the single biggest schematic hole on the defense; a real answer here changes how much help the safeties have to give.
battles.moneyNote: No one in this group carries meaningful guarantees or premium draft capital — Bowman is a Day 3 pick, Henderson/Woods/Bryant/Hall are re-signed role players or reclamations. Nothing financial pre-decides it. Bowman is the widely cited upside pick.

battles.position: WR5 / WR6 (back end of the receiver room)
battles.why: The top four (Drake London, Jahan Dotson, Branch, Olamide Zaccheus) are locked, leaving roughly two spots and six-plus bodies — and a brand-new staff with no history evaluating any of them.
battles.stakes: Special-teams snaps and injury insurance behind London; also the depth that determines whether Atlanta can run three-WR sets without a drop-off.
battles.moneyNote: Every contender is a UDFA, practice-squad graduate or UFL signing with no guaranteed money. The new coaching staff explicitly has no prior attachments here, which removes the usual thumb on the scale for perennial camp standouts Blair and Drummond.

battles.why: Deablo is entrenched at one spot; the other starting job was left open after the offseason additions.
battles.stakes: A starting off-ball linebacker job in a defense that has to hold up against the run in the NFC South.
battles.moneyNote: Harris arrived as the veteran addition and is the favorite; Daniels has not been able to stay healthy, which is the practical disqualifier. Treat the 'competition' framing as courtesy — barring a Harris injury this is his job.

battles.why: The Falcons traded with Kansas City for Wanya Morris in the offseason, which some coverage framed as a left tackle competition.
battles.stakes: Realistically this is a swing-tackle and depth battle, not a starting job — the actual competition is Morris vs. Jerrell vs. Nelson for backup tackle and practice-squad spots.
battles.moneyNote: Jake Matthews remains the projected starting left tackle and Jawaan Taylor the right tackle; Matthews' contract and standing make him effectively unmovable. Morris was Taylor's backup in Kansas City and has, by most evaluations, regressed as a pass protector even as his run blocking improved. If you see 'Falcons LT battle' headlines, the real story is who is the No. 3 tackle.

ATL.biggestUnknown: Michael Penix Jr.'s knee. Everything downstream — whether the QB competition is real or ceremonial, whether Tagovailoa is a bridge or the starter, and whether the new Stefanski/Cunningham regime spends 2026 evaluating Penix or shopping for a 2027 quarterback — depends on how much a player coming off ACL surgery can actually do in August. There is no reporting that resolves it.
ATL.notes:
Structural point that shapes every realness call: Atlanta turned over its entire football operation this offseason (HC Kevin Stefanski, GM Ian Cunningham, president Matt Ryan). A regime change is the one condition under which draft capital stops protecting players — nobody on this roster was drafted by the people making the cuts. That is why the QB battle is credible here and would not be on a team with continuity.

Battles that missed the top five but are live:
- Edge/OLB roster spots: Bralen Trice (2024 third-rounder who has missed both of his NFL seasons with knee injuries and is now healthy), Cameron Thomas (overlapped with Stefanski in Cleveland — a real tiebreaker), DeAngelo Malone (special teams value), Keshawn Banks (UFL signing). Trice's draft capital has effectively expired after two lost years; the team publicly wants him to "show the world who he is," which is encouragement, not a guarantee.
- Backup interior OL: Kyle Hinton, Layden Robinson, Andrew Stueber for likely two spots. Starters are settled — Bergeron LG, Neuzil C, Lindstrom RG (Lindstrom's contract makes him untouchable).
- S4: DeMarcco Hellams vs. Jammie Robinson, with Hellams favored on run-defense need. Jessie Bates III, Xavier Watts and Sydney Brown (acquired from Philadelphia) are the top three.

For a data-driven angle: Atlanta reworked essentially the entire specialist group except long snapper Liam McCullough, so kicker/punter usage is worth watching — but I could not find reporting naming the specific kicker contenders and am not going to invent them.

Caveat on sourcing: nearly every direct article fetch returned HTTP 403 (ESPN, NFL.com, atlantafalcons.com, The Falcoholic, AJC all blocked), so the detail above comes from search-result summaries of those pieces rather than full reads. The broad strokes are consistent across multiple independent outlets; specific depth-chart minutiae (exact nickel rep counts, kicker names) should be re-verified before publication.

battles.position: Base DE / edge opposite Laiatu Latu
battles.why: Tuimoloau washed out of the rotation as a rookie, so the Colts signed Key (and Micheal Clemons) in free agency rather than hand him the job.
battles.stakes: It is the only starting-caliber job on the roster still open, and the pass rush opposite Latu is the difference between a top-10 defense and a middling one.
battles.moneyNote: Tuimoloau's 2025 second-round draft capital gives him the first crack and makes a full demotion unlikely, but Key is on a cheap veteran deal with no guarantee protecting him either — neither contract decides this. The Colts did not spend meaningful capital here again until Day 3 of the 2026 draft, which signals they expect Tuimoloau to win it.

battles.why: Shrader was 13-of-14 before tearing his ACL and MCL in Week 5 of 2025; Grupe replaced him and went 11-of-11 including a franchise-record 60-yarder. Neither man lost the job.
battles.stakes: Whoever loses is likely another team's starting kicker, and the Colts have been churning kickers for years — this is the rare specialist battle with actual league-wide value on both sides.
battles.moneyNote: Both are on cheap one-year deals (Grupe re-signed in March, Shrader is on a minimum-ish deal coming off surgery). There is no guaranteed money anywhere to tilt it. Shrader is the nominal leader only because of health timeline, not contract.

battles.why: Richardson requested a trade, found essentially no market, and returned this spring; the Colts have said they will let him compete with 2025 sixth-rounder Leonard for the backup job.
battles.stakes: Behind a 29-year-old QB eight months removed from an Achilles tear, QB2 is closer to a starting job than usual. Losing it may end Richardson's Colts tenure outright.
battles.moneyNote: Richardson is the No. 4 overall pick of 2023 in the final year of his rookie deal — the draft capital is enormous but it is sunk, and the Colts declining to build around him plus the trade request means it no longer protects him. Leonard is a 2025 sixth-rounder with nothing invested. This is genuinely open in a way high-pick battles usually aren't.

battles.why: Michael Pittman Jr. was traded to Pittsburgh, vacating a large target share behind Alec Pierce and Josh Downs.
battles.stakes: Determines whether the Colts play meaningful 11 personnel or lean harder on tight ends and Jonathan Taylor; Pierce's new deal assumes real WR help exists.
battles.moneyNote: Alec Pierce's four-year, $116M deal and Josh Downs' role lock the top two, so this is strictly for the third spot. Dulin has the inside track on reputation and special-teams value, not money — he is a career special-teamer, not a protected investment. Burks is a 2026 draft pick but a mid/late-round one, so no capital settles it.

battles.why: Local coverage has framed Giddens vs. the rookie McGowan as a camp fight for the change-of-pace role behind Jonathan Taylor.
battles.stakes: Low. Jonathan Taylor absorbs the workload; RB2 matters mainly for injury insurance.
battles.moneyNote: Giddens is a 2025 fifth-round pick with a full season of NFL reps; McGowan is a 2026 seventh-rounder. Seventh-rounders almost never displace an incumbent Day 3 back who is already ahead on the depth chart. Treat this as a depth-and-practice-squad question, not a battle.

IND.notes:
Three more realness calls that didn't make the top five:

- CB4/CB5 roster spots — GENUINE, but fringe. Sauce Gardner, Charvarius Ward and Justin Walley (2025 third-rounder) are locks. Cam Taylor-Britt (one year, $1.402M, no protection), Mekhi Blackmon (784 snaps, 11 starts in his Vikings run), Jaylon Jones, Cameron Mitchell and Johnathan Edwards are fighting for two or three spots. Two or three of them get cut. Nobody in that group has guaranteed money, so it is truly open — it just isn't a starting job.

- Right tackle — LIKELY-SETTLED, borderline media-manufactured. Braden Smith is gone and the Colts have already handed the job to Jalen Travis (2025 fourth-rounder, a few late starts last year), with Blake Freeland and UDFA Nolan Rucci behind him. There is no real competitor on the roster. If anything is unsettled here it is whether Travis is good enough, not who starts.

- Right guard — LIKELY-SETTLED. Matt Goncalves is the starter with 2026 fourth-round pick Jalen Farmer behind him. Rookie fourth-rounders occasionally win guard jobs, so watch it, but Goncalves has the incumbency after replacing Will Fries.

- QB1 — MEDIA-MANUFACTURED if anyone floats it. Daniel Jones signed two years, $88M (up to ~$100M) in March after a top-six season in completion percentage, yards per attempt and passer rating. He is not losing the job in camp under any circumstance short of the Achilles failing.

Two structural facts a data writer should have: the Colts saved roughly $24M in cap by trading Pittman and immediately reinvested it in Pierce ($116M/4yr), so the passing game is now a one-alpha operation. And five of their first six 2026 draft picks were defensive (LB CJ Allen at No. 53, S A.J. Haulcy at No. 78, plus DEs Gumbs and Curry), which tells you where they think the roster is thin — yet almost none of that capital lands in a genuine starting battle, because Latu, Gardner and Ward already occupy the premium defensive spots.

This is also the eighth and final camp at Grand Park in Westfield; camp moves to the Indiana Farm Bureau Football Center in 2027.
IND.biggestUnknown: Daniel Jones' Achilles. He says he is "a full go" for the first practice and expects to be in 11-on-11 immediately, and he did seven-on-sevens by the end of the offseason program — but he tore it in early December and the Colts just committed two years and $88M to him on that basis. Nothing else on this roster is close: a functioning Jones makes the Colts a playoff team with an open kicker job as their biggest problem, and a compromised one hands the season to Anthony Richardson or a sixth-round rookie. Camp practices won't answer it; Week 8 will.
IND.campOpens: Rookies reported Monday, July 27, 2026; veterans reported Tuesday, July 28; first full practice Wednesday, July 29 at Grand Park Sports Campus, Westfield, IN (camp runs through August 20).

battles.why: Mekari was a disappointment in year one in Jacksonville (missed three games, ranked near the bottom of qualifying guards in run-blocking efficiency) and the team spent a 2025 third-rounder on Milum, who is finally healthy after a camp knee injury wiped out his rookie summer.
battles.stakes: Trevor Lawrence's interior protection and the run game in Liam Coen's second year; it is the only starting spot on the line where the incumbent has clearly underperformed his price.
battles.moneyNote: Mekari signed a three-year, $37.5M deal in March 2025, which is the argument for him keeping the job — but he also has swing-tackle value, so the Jaguars can bench him at guard without eating the contract as a pure loss. Milum (2025 Rd 3) and Pregnon (2026 Rd 3, No. 88) are both cheap draft capital pushing him.

battles.position: S (starter opposite Antonio Johnson, plus the third-safety role)
battles.why: Andrew Wingard left for Arizona, opening snaps in a defense that plays a lot of three-safety packages; Ransaw missed his entire rookie year injured and reportedly took over the OTA conversation, and the Jaguars added Huskey on Day 2 specifically for those sub packages.
battles.stakes: Two of the three safety roles are effectively up for grabs, and Jacksonville's dime-heavy structure means the winner plays close to starter snaps regardless of the label.
battles.moneyNote: Ransaw is a 2025 third-round pick the team has never gotten a snap from — that sunk draft capital argues he gets every chance. Huskey was taken at No. 100 in 2026 (some outlets list it as Round 4). Murray is the veteran incumbent with no meaningful guaranteed money left protecting him.

battles.why: Travis Etienne left for New Orleans and the Jaguars deliberately replaced him in the aggregate rather than with one back; Tuten had the whole offseason as the No. 1 while Rodriguez was sidelined for most of the workouts.
battles.stakes: Whether Jacksonville can run the ball at all after letting its lead back walk, and a large fantasy/usage question — this is a true committee unless someone separates.
battles.moneyNote: Rodriguez signed two years, $10M ($12M max) with $6.2M fully guaranteed — that guarantees him a roster spot and real touches, but it is not lead-back money. Tuten is a 2025 Day 3 pick on a rookie deal, so no contract fact decides this; Coen has publicly hyped Tuten for 'a big year,' which is the strongest signal in the room.

battles.why: Pregnon fell to No. 88 despite a consensus top-50 grade and has been developed exclusively on the left side per OC Grant Udinski, which is only worth doing if they intend to play him there.
battles.stakes: Second interior starting job; if Pregnon wins here and Milum wins right guard, Jacksonville rebuilds both guard spots with cheap labor in one camp.
battles.moneyNote: Cleveland is the incumbent veteran and will likely open camp with the job; rookie third-rounders rarely lose a competition on money, but they also rarely unseat a functional veteran before pads. Lean Cleveland Week 1, Pregnon by midseason.

battles.why: Devin Lloyd signed with Carolina and the Jaguars conspicuously did not replace him in free agency or with early draft capital.
battles.stakes: Replacing an All-Pro-caliber coverage linebacker with a run-first player; the coverage drop-off is the most likely place this defense regresses.
battles.moneyNote: No contract or draft capital is competing with Miller — Kiser is a 2025 fourth-rounder, Combs a 2025 UDFA, Hughes a 2026 seventh-rounder. Reporting has consistently framed it as Miller's job to lose since March. Treat any 'open competition' framing in camp as coachspeak.

JAX.biggestUnknown: Travis Hunter's two-way workload. The Jaguars have said repeatedly he is the No. 1 cornerback, but the offensive half is genuinely undecided — he played 67% of snaps before an LCL tear ended his rookie year after seven games, the team then spent two of its 2026 picks on tight ends (Nate Boerkircher in Rd 2, Tanner Koziol in Rd 5), and Coen's scheme leans heavier personnel. Nobody, including the staff, has said how many offensive snaps he gets, and that single number moves the projection for the entire receiver room.
JAX.campOpens: Rookies and quarterbacks reported July 25, 2026; veterans report July 28; first practice July 29 at the Miller Electric Center, camp running through August 26.
JAX.notes:
Things a data-driven writer should know:

1. The WR "battle" is fake as a roster question. Brian Thomas Jr., Travis Hunter, Parker Washington (58/847/5 in 2025, team leader) and Dyami Brown are all locks. What outlets are calling a WR camp battle is really a target-share question, and it is downstream of the Hunter snap decision above — not of anyone winning a job. Classify it media-manufactured if you write it up.

2. TE is settled at the top. Brenton Strange signed an extension this offseason. The interesting sub-plot is that Jacksonville drafted two tight ends (Boerkircher Rd 2, Koziol Rd 5) behind an extended starter, with Johnny Mundt and Hunter Long already on hand — that is a scheme signal (more 12/13 personnel) more than a competition, and it squeezes offensive snaps for Hunter and the WR4.

3. Roster construction context that colors everything: GM James Gladstone made essentially one outside free-agent addition (Chris Rodriguez) and explicitly said he was protecting projected 2027 compensatory picks. Losing Etienne (4yr/$52M to New Orleans) and Devin Lloyd (3yr/$45M to Carolina) with no veteran replacements means the openings at RB and LB are real openings created by choice, not by injury — which is why the internal candidates are so lightly credentialed.

4. Jacksonville had no 2026 first-round pick (traded to Cleveland in the 2025 Hunter deal) and made 10-11 total picks. Gladstone has said publicly he likes carrying a big pick surplus for in-camp and in-season trades — so expect roster churn at the back end, and treat late-camp depth "battles" (No. 3 DE with Danny Striggow, CB5 with Jabbar Muhammad vs. Christian Braswell) as genuinely open but low-stakes.

5. Caution on this brief: several of the best beat sources (SI/Jaguar Report, jaguars.com, ESPN, Big Cat Country, Black and Teal) blocked direct retrieval, so much of the above came through search-result summaries of those articles rather than full text. Directionally I am confident; specific quotes and one detail (whether Jalen Huskey was a third- or fourth-round pick — the team pick list shows No. 100 overall in Round 3, some outlets say Round 4) should be verified before publication.

battles.why: Ikem Ekwonu ruptured his patellar tendon in the playoff game with no return timeline, so the Panthers signed Walker in free agency and then took Freeling at No. 19 overall — two solutions to the same hole.
battles.stakes: It is Bryce Young's blindside in a season where the front office has bet its jobs on Young taking a step forward; get it wrong and the whole offense is compromised.
battles.moneyNote: Walker signed 1 yr / $10M but structured as only ~$4M base plus $6M in incentives — very little dead money if he loses the job. Freeling is the No. 19 overall pick on a 4 yr / $20.9M deal with an $11.6M signing bonus. The draft capital points to Freeling eventually; the reps right now point to Walker.

battles.why: Austin Corbett and Cade Mays are both gone, leaving the pivot genuinely vacant with no incumbent at all.
battles.stakes: Center sets protection calls for a QB whose biggest weakness has been pre-snap and pressure handling; an unsettled center compounds the LT problem next to it.
battles.moneyNote: Neither player is protected. Fortner is on a 1 yr deal worth up to $4.75M (prove-it money, 44 career starts). Hecht is a fifth-rounder, No. 144 overall — the cheapest draft capital in the room. Nothing financial decides this, which is exactly why it is real.

battles.why: Tre'von Moehrig is locked at strong safety, but the other spot is held only by Scott on another one-year veteran deal, with two younger players pushing.
battles.stakes: The last line behind a pass rush that just lost Nic Scourton for the season — coverage has to hold longer now.
battles.moneyNote: Scott is the incumbent purely on a one-year veteran contract with negligible guarantees, which is the classic profile of a placeholder who loses camp. Ransom was a 2025 fourth-rounder who already started six games; Wheatley is a 2026 Day 3 pick out of Penn State who has flashed in camp. Cheap money on all three means this resolves on merit.

battles.why: Rico Dowdle — who took the job from Hubbard midseason — left in free agency, and Brooks is finally healthy after two right ACL tears limited him to nine career carries.
battles.stakes: Dave Canales wants to be run-first; who carries it determines whether the play-action game that protects Young actually functions.
battles.moneyNote: Hubbard is the only one with real contract money (multi-year extension signed in 2024), which gives him a floor but did not stop him losing the job to Dowdle last year. Brooks was a 2024 second-round pick, Etienne a 2025 fourth-rounder — enough capital that the team wants to find out. Reports have Brooks, Hubbard and Etienne all taking first-team reps, which reads more like a committee than a winner-take-all.

battles.why: Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker are set as the top two; the third spot is the only receiver job with any question attached.
battles.stakes: Mostly a snap-share question rather than a job — but it is also the last real referendum on whether Legette was worth a first-round pick.
battles.moneyNote: Legette was the No. 32 overall pick in 2024 and is on a fully guaranteed first-round rookie deal — teams do not bench that in year three off a good camp. Dave Canales has been openly praising him ("having a great camp so far," "he knows the system"), which is the opposite of a coach setting up a demotion. Brazzell is a 2026 rookie who will get snaps, but this is Legette's job unless he loses it outright.

CAR.biggestUnknown: The left side of the offensive line. Ikem Ekwonu's return from a ruptured patellar tendon has no timeline at all, the Panthers spent both a first-round pick (Freeling) and a free-agent contract (Walker) on the same position without declaring a winner, and the center next to them is an open competition between a one-year veteran and a fifth-round rookie. Two of the five OL spots have no settled answer eight weeks from Week 1.
CAR.campOpens: Veterans reported Wednesday, July 22, 2026 — Carolina and Arizona were the first two teams to fully report, because both play in the Hall of Fame Game on Aug. 6. Camp runs July 22 through Aug. 28 at Bank of America Stadium in uptown Charlotte.
CAR.notes:
Things a data-driven writer would want:

1. CAMP IS ALREADY FIVE DAYS OLD. Unlike most teams, Carolina reported July 22 because of the Hall of Fame Game (Aug. 6 vs. Arizona) and four preseason games instead of three. There are already practice reports to work with, and the biggest news has already happened.

2. THE LEAD STORY IS AN INJURY, NOT A BATTLE. Nic Scourton — the 2025 second-round edge rusher — tore his right ACL on the FIRST DAY of practice and is out for the season. Carolina's pass rush finished third-worst in the NFL in sacks (30) in 2025, which is why they signed Jaelan Phillips and drafted Scourton and Princely Umanmielen in the first place. The edge spot opposite Phillips is now genuinely open by subtraction — Umanmielen (2025 third-rounder, 1.5 sacks as a rookie) is the presumed answer, but there is no proven player behind him. I left this off the battle list because the reporting on who is actually competing there is still thin five days in, but it may be the most consequential open job on the roster and is worth a follow-up.

3. TWO BATTLES THE MEDIA IS SELLING THAT AREN'T REAL:
   - LB2 (Trevin Wallace vs. Jackson Kuwatch / Claudin Cherilus). Devin Lloyd's 3 yr / $42M deal locks one spot; Wallace is a 2024 third-rounder returning from injury and is being framed as "not a surefire starter," but a rookie sixth-round-ish linebacker and an undrafted type are not taking a starting job from him. Media-manufactured.
   - CB2 behind Jaycee Horn. Horn and Jackson are described by beat coverage as arguably the best duo in the league. The "competition" is really about who plays nickel and how rookie Will Lee III gets deployed — that is a usage question, not a job battle.

4. CONTRACT ASYMMETRY IS THE TELL ON THE LT BATTLE. Walker's $10M is mostly incentive ($4M base + $6M incentives). That is a structure a team writes when it is not sure the player starts 17 games. Read it as Carolina explicitly buying insurance rather than committing — which makes Freeling's path to the job shorter than the "veteran has the early edge" framing suggests. Watch whether Freeling's second-team reps convert to first-team reps in the Hall of Fame Game.

5. FREELING IS TAKING FIRST-TEAM REPS AT RIGHT TACKLE on Taylor Moton vet days. That is a real signal — it means the coaching staff sees him as a Week 1 starter somewhere, and the LT/RT question may resolve as "Freeling starts, at whichever side."

6. UNVERIFIED ITEM: one source described Chris Brazzell II as a second-round pick, but Carolina's listed 2026 second-rounder is DT Lee Hunter, who was the only draftee still unsigned as of the signing report. Confirm Brazzell's round before printing it.

7. Confidence is medium rather than high because panthers.com, ESPN and SI all returned 403 to direct fetches, so this is assembled from search-result summaries of those pieces rather than full text. The camp-opening facts, the Scourton injury, the Freeling/Walker and Fortner/Hecht competitions, and the contract figures were each corroborated across more than one source. Some safety-room detail in circulating coverage mixes 2025 and 2026 context — treat the Nick Scott/Ransom/Wheatley ordering as directional.

8. No kicker or specialist battle surfaced in any reporting. Trevor Etienne was the primary return man as a rookie.

battles.position: S2 (free safety, opposite Dante Trader Jr.)
battles.why: Miami has no returning starter opposite Trader and nobody in the room has meaningful guaranteed money or draft capital — it is a career special-teamer, a journeyman, a fifth-round rookie and a UDFA all starting from zero.
battles.stakes: Hafley's defense leans on two-high structures and interchangeable safeties; whoever wins is on the field for most of the snaps in a scheme built around post-safety discipline.
battles.moneyNote: No one here is protected: Anderson and Johnson are veteran-minimum types, Taaffe was a 2026 fifth-round pick (Texas), Moore is an undrafted rookie from Indiana. Zero guaranteed money argues the job is truly won on the grass. Anderson's edge is scheme familiarity from Hafley's Green Bay years, not contract.

battles.position: WR (essentially every spot after the slot)
battles.why: Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle are both gone and the replacements are journeyman free agents and Day 3 rookies — there is no established No. 1 and no depth-chart inertia to overcome.
battles.stakes: This decides whether Malik Willis has anything resembling a passing game in year one of the rebuild, and it sets the target hierarchy for a full season.
battles.moneyNote: Tolbert and Atwell are on modest short-term veteran deals with little dead money — cutting or benching either is painless. Washington is a 2024 sixth-rounder on a rookie deal. Nobody in the room has the kind of guarantee that buys snaps, which is exactly why this one is real.

battles.why: Patterson is the incumbent off the most accurate single season in franchise history, but he is historically weak from 50+ (roughly 7-of-13 career) and Miami signed Gonzalez in free agency specifically to contest the job.
battles.stakes: A one-man roster spot with no fallback; in a rebuilding year decided by close games, leg strength on kickoffs and long field goals is a real swing.
battles.moneyNote: Both are on cheap one-year veteran deals — neither contract creates any incentive to keep the loser. Gonzalez reportedly has history with Miami's new special teams staff, which is the only thumb on the scale.

battles.why: Savaiinaea struggled at left guard as a rookie in 2025 and is sliding back to his natural right side, and the new staff has publicly committed to open competition everywhere.
battles.stakes: Miami is pivoting to a heavier, possession-style run game; the right guard/right tackle pairing is where that identity either works or doesn't.
battles.moneyNote: Savaiinaea was a 2025 second-round pick on a four-year rookie deal in his second season — teams almost never bench that capital in August for a sixth-round rookie. Campbell (2026 sixth round) is the pressure, not the favorite. Treat the reps as development, not a real coin flip.

battles.why: Ewers finished 2025 as the starter and has reportedly impressed Hafley through the offseason, so the local coverage keeps framing it as a competition.
battles.stakes: It is the franchise's entire direction — whether the rebuild is being built around the free agent they paid or the young passer already on the roster.
battles.moneyNote: Willis signed a three-year, $67.5M deal as the hand-picked choice of GM Jon-Eric Sullivan and HC Jeff Hafley. That money and that authorship make him the Week 1 starter barring injury. Ewers is a legitimate QB2 and the in-season contingency, but this is not an open camp battle — closer to media-manufactured than the coverage admits.

MIA.biggestUnknown: The wide receiver room. With Hill and Waddle both gone and no replacement carrying guaranteed money or first-round capital, Miami genuinely does not know who its No. 1, No. 2 or No. 3 receiver is — and that uncertainty cascades into every evaluation of Malik Willis. Several outlets called it the most unsettled receiver room in the AFC East, and that reads as accurate rather than hyperbolic.
MIA.campOpens: Rookies reported July 21, 2026; veterans report Tuesday, July 28, 2026. Camp runs July 28 through Aug. 26 at the Baptist Health Training Complex in Miami Gardens, with the first public practice Sunday, Aug. 2.
MIA.notes:
Context a data-driven writer should have: this is a full teardown. New HC Jeff Hafley and new GM Jon-Eric Sullivan are running their first camp, and Tua Tagovailoa, Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle are all gone. That means unusually few positions are locked by incumbency — but also that the few players who WERE paid or drafted high are effectively untouchable, which is what separates the genuine battles from the manufactured ones here.

Draft capital that pre-decides jobs: Miami had two first-round picks. OT/OG Kadyn Proctor went No. 12 overall (Alabama, 40 career starts at LT) and CB Chris Johnson went No. 27 (San Diego State) after a trade up with San Francisco. Both are starters on arrival — any "competition" involving them is developmental. The open question with Proctor is positional, not competitive: he is being moved inside to left guard with Patrick Paul (2024 second-rounder, 17 starts in 2025) at LT and Austin Jackson at RT. If Jackson's injury history repeats, Proctor kicking back outside is the likelier fix than a true camp battle.

Positions I deliberately did NOT list as battles: RB1 is closed — De'Von Achane signed a four-year, ~$64M extension. The RB2 job behind him (Ollie Gordon II and others) is genuinely open but is a low-leverage touches battle, not a roster-defining one. Center is closed — Aaron Brewer is an All-Pro and was a finalist for the inaugural Protector of the Year award. ILB is closed — All-Pro Jordyn Brooks anchors a veteran room.

One caution on secondary reporting: several aggregators conflated the safety competition with a cornerback competition, listing Lonnie Johnson Jr., Zayne Anderson, Louis Moore and Michael Taaffe as fighting for a spot "next to Dante Trader Jr." Trader is a safety, so that is the safety job, not CB2. CB2 opposite Chris Johnson is a real question I could not source cleanly and did not want to invent contenders for.

Methodology caveat: ESPN, SI/OnSI, the team site and AtoZ Sports all returned HTTP 403 to direct fetches, so the details above come from search-result summaries of those pieces plus Phinsider and DolphinsTalk. The structural facts (contracts, draft slots, camp dates) corroborate across multiple sources and I am confident in them; some individual name-level depth chart details are second-hand, which is why confidence is medium rather than high.

battles.why: Stafford, the reigning MVP, is on a modified camp rep plan and did not practice on Day 1, handing all the work to Simpson and Bennett, and neither reportedly separated in the spring.
battles.stakes: Stafford is at the end of his career and the Rams are in Super Bowl-or-bust mode; whoever wins QB2 is one hamstring away from running a title contender's offense, and the rep split also sets the pace of the succession plan.
battles.moneyNote: Simpson was the No. 13 overall pick in the 2026 draft and signed a fully guaranteed first-round rookie deal — that capital makes him the eventual starter no matter what happens in August, but reporting out of OTAs had Bennett (2023 fourth-rounder, cheap expiring deal) as the current leader for the 2026 backup job. Draft capital decides the job in 2027, not necessarily Week 1 of 2026.

battles.why: Davante Adams and Puka Nacua are locked in as the top two, and the No. 3 job behind them is unclaimed — sources disagree on whether it's Whittington/Smith or the two young draftees, which is itself evidence nobody has won it.
battles.stakes: McVay's offense runs heavy 11 personnel, so WR3 is close to a starter's snap count; it also determines whether a fifth receiver survives the 53-man cut.
battles.moneyNote: No meaningful money or draft capital anywhere in the group — Mumpfield was a 2025 seventh-rounder, Daniels a 2026 sixth-rounder, Whittington a 2024 sixth-rounder. Nothing is protecting any of them, which is exactly why it is open. Mumpfield is a real cut candidate if the Rams keep only five WRs.

battles.why: Kyren Williams is the entrenched starter, but Hunter played zero offensive snaps as a rookie (special teams only) and Year 2 is historically when McVay's backs break through; Corum has to hold him off.
battles.stakes: Determines the change-of-pace and goal-line role, and who insures a heavy-usage starter in Williams.
battles.moneyNote: Corum was a 2024 third-round pick, Hunter a 2025 fourth-rounder — close enough in capital that neither is protected. Williams' RB1 job is not in play.

battles.why: The starting five is set and returning largely intact, but the backup interior spots behind them are genuinely unresolved — Limmer has scheme experience but struggled filling in at guard last year, and the Rams brought Quessenberry back rather than commit to the young players.
battles.stakes: Low-glamour but real: it decides who protects a 38-year-old MVP quarterback when a starter goes down, and it decides two or three 53-man spots.
battles.moneyNote: No guarantees or premium capital in this group — these are late-round and veteran-minimum bodies, so it will be settled on August practice tape. Kevin Dotson at RG and the rest of the starting five are not part of this.

battles.why: Media framing treats the reshuffled corner room as open, but the Rams traded for Trent McDuffie in March and signed Jaylen Watson, and Lake has held the slot; Forbes is described by team-side coverage as the top backup, not a challenger.
battles.stakes: Depth and sub-package snaps on a defense that is now the team's identity after the Myles Garrett trade.
battles.moneyNote: The Rams surrendered real trade capital for All-Pro Trent McDuffie and paid Jaylen Watson in free agency — teams do not bench acquisitions like that in camp. Forbes' 2023 first-round capital came from Washington, not the Rams, so it carries no protection here.

LA.biggestUnknown: The quarterback room behind Matthew Stafford. Stafford is the reigning MVP but is on a deliberately limited camp rep plan and sat out the first practice, so the Rams genuinely do not know yet whether Ty Simpson (No. 13 overall) is ready to be the emergency answer in 2026 or whether Stetson Bennett is still the safer hand — and reporting from OTAs suggested neither has seized it. Everything else on this roster is depth-tier; this is the only unsettled thing that could decide the season.
LA.campOpens: Veterans reported Saturday, July 25, 2026; on-field camp runs July 26 – Aug. 7 at Loyola Marymount University in Los Angeles.
LA.notes:
Things a data-driven writer should know, several of which cut against the obvious storylines:

1. This is a top-heavy, closed roster. The Rams traded for Trent McDuffie (March) and reigning DPOY Myles Garrett (June) after losing the NFC Championship Game to Seattle. Those two acquisitions plus Jared Verse and Byron Young mean the edge and outside-corner spots that would normally generate camp stories are completely settled by acquisition cost. There are fewer genuine battles here than on a typical roster, and none of them are starting jobs.

2. Kicker is NOT a battle, despite it being one the last two summers. Harrison Mevis took the job from Joshua Karty midseason in 2025 (Karty was waived), went 12-for-13 in the regular season and hit the OT game-winner against Chicago in the playoffs. The Rams brought in no competition for him this summer. If you see a Rams kicker-battle item, it is recycled 2025 content.

3. Linebacker is the roster's weakest position but is not an open competition. Nate Landman and Omar Speights are the starters, with Grant Stuard and Shaun Dolac behind them. The gap between "weak spot" and "competition" is the story here — the Rams appear to have decided to live with it rather than compete it out.

4. The real Rams story this camp is contracts, not battles. Puka Nacua, Kobie Turner, Byron Young and Steve Avila — the entire core of the 2023 draft class — are all entering the final year of their rookie deals, and McVay has confirmed "internal dialogue" about extensions. That is a bigger 2026 roster variable than any camp rep count.

5. Conflicting WR3 reporting is a signal, not noise. Some outlets frame it as Jordan Whittington vs. Xavier Smith; others as Konata Mumpfield vs. CJ Daniels. When beat coverage can't agree on who the contenders even are, the job is genuinely unassigned.

6. Methodology caveat: direct article fetches were blocked (HTTP 403) across ESPN, SI/Ram Digest, Turf Show Times, therams.com and the LA Times syndication, so this is assembled from search-result summaries of those outlets rather than full reads. The camp dates, the trades, the QB competition and the kicker status are corroborated across multiple independent sources; the OL depth and WR3 contender lists are single-source and should be re-verified before publication.

CHI.campOpens: Rookies reported Saturday, July 25, 2026; veterans report Tuesday, July 28, 2026. First practice July 29, first fan-open practice July 31, at Halas Hall (Lake Forest, IL).

battles.why: Pro Bowl center Drew Dalman abruptly retired in the spring, blowing a hole in the middle of the line; Chicago responded by trading for Bradbury and spending the No. 57 pick on Jones.
battles.stakes: Caleb Williams' protection calls and the run game run through the pivot; Ben Johnson's offense leans hard on a center who can make the line calls and reach-block in the zone scheme.
battles.moneyNote: Logan Jones was the 57th pick (2nd round, 2026) — Rimington Trophy winner, and at 24/25 he is old for a rookie, which is exactly the profile teams start immediately. Bradbury arrived by trade, not a big free-agent contract, so there is no guaranteed money protecting him. Johnson has publicly said he values a veteran at center, which points to Bradbury Week 1, but the draft capital points to Jones by midseason. This is the one Bears battle where the money does NOT pre-decide it.

battles.why: Stevenson has never locked down the job opposite Jaylon Johnson and the front office declined to extend him; the Bears spent a 2026 fourth-rounder on Muhammad and Smith is healthy again.
battles.stakes: With Jaylon Johnson coming off a down year and Kyler Gordon locked into the slot, CB2 is the last soft spot in a secondary the Bears otherwise spent heavily to fix.
battles.moneyNote: Stevenson is in the final year of his 2023 second-round rookie deal with no extension — the strongest possible tell that the team is not committed to him. Muhammad is only a fourth-rounder (2026), i.e. cheap, low-capital, and easy to bench if he loses — which is what makes this a real, two-way competition rather than a coronation. Zah Frazier (2025 5th) was released, thinning the field.

battles.why: Ozzy Trapilo, the presumed 2026 starter, tore a patellar tendon in the playoffs, forcing the Bears to re-open the job and re-sign Braxton Jones.
battles.stakes: Caleb Williams' blind side. If Jones' health holds this is a non-issue; if it doesn't, the Bears are down to two players who haven't taken meaningful LT snaps in over a year.
battles.moneyNote: Jones was re-signed to a one-year, $5M deal specifically to be the starter and took every first-team rep in the spring with a clean bill of health and 44 career starts. Wills and Amegadjie (2024 3rd round) are not locks to even make the 53. Treat national 'wide-open left tackle race' framing skeptically — some of it is recycled 2025 copy that still lists Trapilo as an active competitor. The real question here is Jones' durability, not the depth chart.

battles.why: Odeyingbo underdelivered on his contract in year one and Booker surged late in 2025 (4.5 sacks, 12 QB hits in the second half), so beat writers have framed it as a three-man start.
battles.stakes: Chicago's pass rush was the stated priority of the offseason; if nobody wins this outright, Sweat is again the only credible rusher on the roster.
battles.moneyNote: Odeyingbo signed a three-year, $48M deal — a contract of that size does not lose a camp battle for the Week 1 start, whatever the practice reps suggest. What IS genuinely open is the snap split: Booker (2024 5th-rounder, cheap) and Turner (2025 2nd-rounder) can take rotational passing-down work away from Odeyingbo without the Bears ever changing the starting lineup card. Track snap share, not the depth chart.

battles.why: DJ Moore was traded to Buffalo, leaving a vacancy behind Rome Odunze and Luther Burden III with no established third option on the roster.
battles.stakes: Determines who gets the No. 3 target share in a Ben Johnson offense that historically feeds a movable slot/gadget receiver, plus the return job.
battles.moneyNote: No meaningful guaranteed money or draft capital in the room — Raymond is a veteran special-teams signing and Thomas a late-round rookie, so this is decided on merit. Raymond's edge is scheme familiarity: he played for Ben Johnson in Detroit from 2022-24, which is a real thumb on the scale in a first-team-reps sense. Caveat: 'WR3' here mostly means return man plus 25-30 snaps a game, not a fantasy-relevant role.

CHI.biggestUnknown: The interior and left edge of the offensive line. Drew Dalman retired in the spring and Ozzy Trapilo tore a patellar tendon in the playoffs, so the two spots the Bears thought were settled in January are the two they're rebuilding in July — a traded-for veteran center or a rookie second-rounder snapping the ball, and a left tackle on a one-year prove-it deal with a durability history. Everything about Caleb Williams' year-three leap depends on how those two spots resolve, and neither has a contract or a draft pick large enough to have pre-decided it.
CHI.notes:
Things a data-driven writer would want that didn't make the top five:

1) The safety "battle" is not one. Coby Bryant (free-agent signing, four INTs and seven PBUs for the Super Bowl-winning Seahawks in 2025) and Dillon Thieneman (No. 25 overall, 2026) are the starters. Any framing of this as a competition is media-manufactured — a first-round pick and a just-signed veteran do not lose jobs in July. Worth writing about as a snap-role question (Thieneman ran 4.35 and can play nickel, so the interesting data question is how often Chicago plays big nickel with him in the slot), not a starter question.

2) There is a genuine, real competition at long snapper: rookie Beau Gardner vs. second-year Luke Elkin, the last two college All-American snappers. Trivial for the team, but it is one of the few spots on the roster where nothing has been pre-decided. Cairo Santos and Tory Taylor are locks.

3) Roster-bubble stories that are more real than most "battles": Roschon Johnson survived the RB cut last year by a thread and may not if Chicago keeps only three backs; at linebacker, Tremaine Edmunds was cut for cap savings and replaced by Devin Bush, which puts Ruben Hyppolite II (2025 4th) genuinely at risk behind Jack Sanborn's special-teams value and Tony Fields II.

4) Methodological caution for anyone scraping this: a nontrivial amount of "2026 Bears position battle" content circulating right now is recycled 2025 copy. The clearest tell is articles still listing Ozzy Trapilo as an active LT competitor when July 2026 reporting has him recovering from a torn patellar tendon suffered in the playoffs. Date-filter aggressively and prefer Shaw Local, the Sun-Times, chicagobears.com, and ProFootballRumors over the SI/FanSided network for this team.

5) The pattern across this roster: Chicago spent real money and real capital at safety, DE, and center this offseason, which means most of the "battles" are actually snap-share questions with pre-determined starters. The exceptions — center, CB2, WR3 — are exactly the three spots where the incumbent has neither guaranteed money nor high draft capital.

battles.why: DJ Turner II and Dax Hill are locked on the boundary, but the slot job was never claimed — Davis is a career journeyman incumbent and the Bengals brought in Taylor, a slot specialist, specifically to push him.
battles.stakes: Cincinnati plays heavy nickel; this is effectively a third starting corner job on a defense that has to hold up while the pass rush rebuilds without Hendrickson.
battles.moneyNote: Nobody in the group has leverage money: Taylor signed a one-year deal on April 2 as a former sixth-rounder, Davis is a low-cost veteran, Lux and Newton are late-round/UDFA types. Beat coverage from OTAs had Taylor taking first-team 7-on-7 reps, which is exactly what an open job looks like. Multiple Bengals writers called it the only true starting battle on the roster.

battles.position: Starting DE opposite Boye Mafe (and the pass-rush rotation order)
battles.why: Trey Hendrickson signed with Baltimore (4 yr / $112M), vacating the only settled edge role; Mafe was signed to take one spot and the other is genuinely unassigned among three recent premium picks.
battles.stakes: This is the whole season. The Bengals bet that volume of draft capital plus Mafe replaces a four-time Pro Bowl edge; if it doesn't, Al Golden's defense wastes another Joe Burrow year.
battles.moneyNote: Draft capital is stacked on both sides, which is why nobody can be crowned: Murphy was the 2023 first-rounder (No. 28), Stewart the 2025 first-rounder (No. 17, fully guaranteed rookie deal), Howell the 2026 second-rounder. Mafe's free-agent contract makes his own snaps safe, so treat only the second job and the rotation order as open. Stewart's guaranteed first-round money means he will get every chance regardless of camp reps — he holds a floor, not the job.

battles.why: Chase and Higgins are untouchable but the third spot has been an open audition for two years; the Bengals used a 2026 fourth-rounder on Young, who is 6-5 and has drawn OTA buzz.
battles.stakes: In an offense that funnels everything to two receivers, WR3 is the release valve on third down and in the red zone — and the swing snaps if Higgins misses time again, which he has every year.
battles.moneyNote: No contract protects the incumbent: Iosivas is a 2023 sixth-round pick playing out a rookie deal at near-minimum money. Young's fourth-round capital is real but not the kind that buys a job. Tinsley has the scheme-familiarity edge. Iosivas is the favorite on continuity alone, not on money — this can genuinely flip in August.

battles.why: Cincinnati signed Dugger in April after Cook, and the presence of a decorated veteran behind a young incumbent reads like a competition.
battles.stakes: Golden's structure asks a lot of the second safety in the run fit; a downgrade shows up immediately against Baltimore and Pittsburgh.
battles.moneyNote: Cook's three-year, $40.25M deal ($18M in year one) settles the top safety spot outright. Dugger signed only a one-year prove-it contract on April 2 — that is third-safety/sub-package money, not starter money. Battle entered camp as the starter after a 125-tackle season and local reporting frames it as 'not up for debate.' Expect Dugger to take real snaps as a big-nickel/dime piece rather than to take the job.

battles.why: The Bengals spent a 2026 fourth-rounder on Lew and Karras is 33 and in the final year of his deal, so the succession question is live even if this season's answer is not.
battles.stakes: Karras has been the most consistent piece of Burrow's protection for four years; the Bengals return all five 2025 starters and continuity is the entire premise of the 2026 line.
battles.moneyNote: Karras is the incumbent starter and the Bengals publicly framed 2026 as bringing back all five starting linemen — the first time in the Burrow era. Lew is coming off a torn ACL at Auburn and only just avoided a camp-opening injury list; fourth-round capital does not unseat a proven starter in August. Read Lew as the 2027 starter and this camp as a redshirt-with-reps, not a battle.

CIN.biggestUnknown: Whether the post-Hendrickson pass rush is actually a pass rush. The Bengals replaced a four-time Pro Bowler with Boye Mafe plus a pile of unproven draft capital, and the single biggest variable is Shemar Stewart — a 2025 top-20 pick whose rookie year was consumed by a contract holdout and then a knee injury, leaving the team with essentially no evidence about a player it needs to be a starter.
CIN.campOpens: Rookies reported Saturday, July 25, 2026; veterans report Tuesday, July 28, with the first full practice Wednesday, July 29 (Paycor Stadium / Kettering Health Practice Fields, Cincinnati).
CIN.notes:
Context that shapes every judgment above: Cincinnati spent this offseason buying certainty everywhere except edge. They traded for Dexter Lawrence II and extended him (one year, $28M through 2028), signed Jonathan Allen (two years, $26M, up to $28M with incentives), and gave Bryan Cook three years/$40.25M. That is a lot of guaranteed interior money, which means the DL interior is closed and the only defensive-front question is who rushes off the edge. Trey Hendrickson was allowed to walk to Baltimore rather than be tagged at $24.434M — the Bengals are now living with that decision.

Two storylines to be skeptical of. First, tight end. Mike Gesicki vs. Erick All Jr. vs. Drew Sample vs. Tanner Hudson vs. rookie Jack Endries gets written up as a battle every summer; Gesicki's extension money and role make him the pass-catching TE1, and All's upside is a snap-share question, not a job question. I left it off the list as closer to media-manufactured than genuine. Second, the offensive line generally: Orlando Brown Jr. was extended through 2028 in March, Dalton Risner returns at right guard, Dylan Fairchild is the entrenched left guard despite mediocre 2025 PFF grades (46th of 81 guards), and Amarius Mims is a former first-rounder. Any "OL competition" framing this August is noise.

Also settled and worth not chasing: kicker (Evan McPherson is under contract through 2027) and backup QB (Joe Flacco re-signed one year on March 25).

For a data-driven angle: the Bengals' 2026 edge room is four-deep in draft capital with almost no NFL production behind it — Mafe's Seattle sack totals plus Murphy's three years of underperformance against his draft slot is a clean, quantifiable "capital vs. output" story. And the slot corner battle is a rare genuinely open starting job where neither contender has ever been a full-time starter, which is unusual for a team with playoff expectations.

Methodological caveat: WebFetch was blocked (HTTP 403) on essentially every major outlet — ESPN, NFL.com, Yahoo, bengals.com, Cincy Jungle, atozsports — so the above is assembled from search-result summaries of those pieces rather than full-article reads. The consensus across independent outlets was consistent, but exact contract figures and quote attributions should be spot-checked before publication. Confidence is medium for that reason, not because the reporting is thin.

battles.why: David Edwards left in free agency, leaving the only opening on an otherwise-returning offensive line, and the Bills brought in a veteran plus two drafted guards rather than anointing anyone.
battles.stakes: It is the one hole in front of Josh Allen on a line that is otherwise the most stable unit on the offense, and it is the first real personnel call of the Joe Brady head-coaching era.
battles.moneyNote: Corbett is a low-cost veteran free-agent add (9th season, age 30) with no meaningful guarantee reported; Anderson is a cheap former UDFA on a minimum-level deal. Neither has money that decides it. Buffalo also spent the 102nd pick on Jude Bowry (4th round) and a 7th on Ar'maj Reed-Adams. Separately, incumbent RG O'Cyrus Torrence is in the final year of his rookie deal at a $4.31M cap hit. Buffalo News called LG the team's biggest camp battle; projections split between Corbett and Anderson, which is itself evidence it is open.

battles.position: ILB2 (inside linebacker next to Terrel Bernard)
battles.why: The switch to Jim Leonhard's 3-4 raises the value of the second off-ball linebacker, and Williams — who had the job to lose — was hurt this offseason, opening the door for the rookie.
battles.stakes: A full-time defensive starter in a brand-new scheme; whoever wins is on the field for the majority of base snaps in a defense with no returning identity.
battles.moneyNote: Williams is a 2023 third-round pick now at the end of his rookie deal, so there is no guaranteed money protecting him. Elarms-Orr is a 2026 fourth-rounder — real but not decisive capital. Brady said Williams should be ready by the start of camp, which keeps this a true two-man race rather than a default handoff.

battles.position: DL3 (third defensive line starter in the 3-4)
battles.why: Leonhard is rebuilding the front from scratch; Ed Oliver and Deone Walker are treated as locks, and the third spot in the three-man front belongs to nobody.
battles.stakes: The last starting job on a defensive front that has to justify the entire scheme change; it also determines whether Buffalo's 2025 defensive line draft class was worth it.
battles.moneyNote: Sanders enters ahead on capital — Buffalo traded up to No. 41 in 2025 to get him — but he lost his rookie year to a knee injury (IR in October), so this is effectively his first real camp and the tape does not back the capital yet. Landon Jackson (2025 third round) also lost his rookie season to a knee injury and, per local reporting, is not even guaranteed a 2026 roster spot. Durant is the cheapest of the three. Draft capital tilts this toward Sanders but has not settled it.

battles.why: Hairston's rookie year was wrecked by injuries, so beat writers frame the job as re-openable, and Buffalo drafted Igbinosun out of Ohio State to add competition.
battles.stakes: A full-time starting outside corner in a new coverage scheme, on a defense with essentially no continuity.
battles.moneyNote: Hairston was Buffalo's 2025 first-round pick (No. 30) on a fully guaranteed four-year rookie contract with a fifth-year option — first-round corners in year two effectively never lose camp jobs to a rookie. Brandon Beane said publicly after the 2026 draft that Benford and Hairston are penciled in as the boundary starters. Treat the 'battle' as real pressure on Hairston's snap count, not a real threat to the starting job unless he is hurt again. (I could not confirm Igbinosun's exact draft round — Buffalo's 2026 second-rounder went to Chicago in the DJ Moore trade, so some outlets' 'second-round rookie' label is suspect.)

battles.why: DJ Moore and Khalil Shakir are locked in as WR1/WR2, and Coleman has not held the third role convincingly — 38 catches, 404 yards over 13 games in 2025 after a big Week 1.
battles.stakes: How Brady and Pete Carmichael build the passing game around Allen; the WR3 snaps are the difference between a two-man receiving corps and a real one.
battles.moneyNote: Important caveat: Palmer carries roughly $14.2M in dead money, which makes him effectively uncuttable and likely guarantees him snaps regardless of camp — so the *roster* question is settled even though the *snap* question is not. Coleman is a 2024 second-round pick still on his rookie deal, so his capital is real but not protective. Bell is a 2026 fourth-rounder (4.40 speed) who reportedly flashed in the offseason program. The honest read: Coleman opens as WR3, Palmer plays anyway because of the money, Bell is the one who can actually change the order.

BUF.notes:
Context that matters more than any individual battle: this is a new-regime camp. Sean McDermott is out; Joe Brady is the head coach, Pete Carmichael is running the offense, and Jim Leonhard (from Denver, which led the NFL with 68 sacks) is the new defensive coordinator converting Buffalo from McDermott's nine-year 4-3 to a 3-4. That means almost every "battle" on defense is really a scheme-fit question — the depth chart is being redrawn, not competed for in the usual sense. Brady has said he wants camp to be "extremely tough"; practices moved up about an hour and 15 minutes from McDermott's schedule, there are fewer Pittsford practices (seven), and one extra public session at the new stadium.

Two things the media is calling battles that are not:
- Kicker. Tyler Bass missed all of 2025 and is currently the ONLY kicker on the 90-man roster. There is literally no competitor in the building. Any "kicker battle" framing is manufactured; if Bass struggles the Bills will *add* someone, but that is not a camp battle going in.
- Running back. James Cook won the 2025 rushing title and is signed; Ty Johnson and Ray Davis fill out the room. The "third-down back" storyline is a snap-share question, not a roster question.

Other real-but-secondary items: the safety pecking order (Cole Bishop is treated as a locked starter, which squeezes Damar Hamlin), TE3, and the last two or three OL roster spots. Also worth flagging for a data-driven piece: Buffalo traded its 2026 second-round pick to Chicago for DJ Moore (plus a fifth), which is why the draft-capital picture on defense is thinner than usual and why so many 2025 draftees are being asked to win jobs immediately.

Data caveat: WebFetch returned HTTP 403 on essentially every source (ESPN, Buffalo News, Buffalo Rumblings, SI, WIVB, Niagara Gazette, Yahoo), so this is assembled from search-result summaries rather than full article text. Several summaries visibly blended 2025 and 2026 offseason content (e.g. Taron Johnson / Tre'Davious White / Jordan Poyer departures and Dee Alford / C.J. Gardner-Johnson / Geno Stone signings appear in a "2026" secondary summary but describe an earlier offseason). I have excluded anything I could not corroborate across two 2026-dated sources.
BUF.biggestUnknown: Whether the defense actually functions in Jim Leonhard's 3-4. Buffalo ran McDermott's scheme for nine years and is now rebuilding the front seven from scratch with a first-year head coach, a converted 3-4 front, unproven 2025 draftees (T.J. Sanders, Landon Jackson) coming off lost rookie seasons, and position switches (Joey Bosa moving on the front). Three of the five camp battles above are downstream of that one question — until the scheme takes, no defensive depth chart on this roster means much.
BUF.campOpens: Rookies reported July 21, 2026; veterans reported July 28; first full practice Wednesday, July 29 at St. John Fisher University in Pittsford, NY. Seven public Pittsford practices run July 29 - Aug. 7 (all 8:30 a.m.), plus an added public session at the new stadium.

KC.campOpens: Rookies and QBs reported Fri July 24; veterans reported July 28; camp runs July 28/29 through Aug 20 at Missouri Western State University, St. Joseph, MO (16th year there). First open practice July 29 (season-ticket holders only).

battles.why: Kansas City traded up to No. 6 for Mansoor Delane to lock one boundary spot, then stacked three plausible veterans/young starters on the other side with no incumbent clearly established.
battles.stakes: Spagnuolo's man-heavy pressure looks require two corners who can survive alone; this is the difference between blitzing freely and playing scared.
battles.moneyNote: Delane (No. 6 overall, highest KC pick since 2013) is untouchable — the battle is only for the spot opposite him. Sneed is a re-signed veteran on a reset deal rather than the big-money contract he had in Tennessee, so none of the three has a guarantee large enough to decide it; ESPN's Nate Taylor has flagged this as camp's top competition.

battles.why: Jawaan Taylor is gone (released, now in Atlanta), leaving the only unsettled spot on an otherwise set line (Simmons LT, Sumataia LG, Humphrey C, Smith RG).
battles.stakes: It is the last hole in front of a quarterback coming off ACL/LCL reconstruction — the single most consequential protection question on the roster.
battles.moneyNote: Moore is in year two of a two-year, $30M deal signed in 2025 — but the bulk of that guarantee was 2025 money, and he already lost the LT job he was signed for to rookie Josh Simmons, starting only six games. Pole is a 2025 UDFA (Washington State) with zero capital, yet took first-team reps in OTAs. KC also declined to spend meaningful draft capital on a tackle in 2026, which is the strongest single signal that they believe the answer is already in the building.

battles.why: Chamarri Conner is moving from nickel back to safety to replace Bryan Cook (lost in free agency), vacating the slot outright.
battles.stakes: KC plays nickel as its base personnel; whoever wins is effectively a starter, and the loser of the safety domino makes it worse if Conner struggles.
battles.moneyNote: Kohou signed as a free agent coming off an ACL tear — a modest prove-it deal, not a contract that guarantees snaps. Canady is a 2026 fourth-rounder: enough capital to get a long look, not enough to be handed the job.

battles.why: Rice, Worthy and Tyquan Thornton are the settled top three; everything behind them is open, and Rice/Worthy availability history means the WR4 will play real snaps.
battles.stakes: Insurance. If either of the top two misses time again, the camp winner becomes a starter by default.
battles.moneyNote: Rice and Worthy are first/second-round investments and are not losing starting jobs regardless of camp; Allen is a 2026 Day 3 rookie, Royals a 2025 Day 3 pick — all cheap, all genuinely interchangeable.

battles.why: Framed as a competition because Mahomes is coming off knee surgery and the Chiefs both traded for Fields and drafted Nussmeier in the same offseason.
battles.stakes: Only matters if Mahomes' knee doesn't hold — but in that scenario it matters enormously.
battles.moneyNote: Fields was acquired by trade from the Jets specifically to be the primary backup and carries the salary to match. Nussmeier was pick No. 249 (seventh round, via Pittsburgh); ESPN's Nate Taylor reported he should treat 2026 as a redshirt year. Seventh-rounders do not beat out traded-for veterans in August.

KC.biggestUnknown: Patrick Mahomes' left knee. He tore the ACL and LCL in Week 15 against the Chargers, and although Andy Reid cleared him for full participation and he opened camp in a brace without incident, nobody — including the Chiefs — knows how much of his off-platform, extend-the-play movement comes back by the Week 1 opener at Denver on Sept. 14. Every other question on this roster is downstream of that one.
KC.notes: Three things a data-driven writer should chew on. (1) The Chiefs went cornerback-first in a way they never do — trading up to No. 6 for Delane, adding Kohou, Fulton and a returning Sneed, and drafting Canady in the fourth. That is four acquisitions at one position group in one offseason, which usually signals the front office had no confidence in the room rather than a genuine open competition. (2) The right tackle situation is the rare case where money points the wrong way: Moore's $30M deal is a sunk 2025 guarantee, and the same regime that paid him watched a rookie take his job last year. An undrafted second-year player getting first-team OTA reps against a $15M-a-year veteran is a real signal, not a hype cycle. (3) The safety chain reaction is underreported — losing Bryan Cook forced Conner off the nickel, which is what created the slot battle in the first place. Alohi Gilman is the assumed replacement, but if that pairing doesn't work KC has two holes, not one. Also worth tracking: RB2/RB3 between rookie Emmett Johnson and free-agent Emari Demercado, and a crowded TE room behind Kelce/Gray where Jared Wiley, Jake Briningstool (injury question) and rookie John Michael Gyllenborg are fighting for one spot.

battles.why: Kevin O'Connell publicly declared an open competition and left minicamp without naming a starter, and has set no decision timeline; multiple outlets report Murray outperformed McCarthy through the spring while O'Connell says McCarthy also had a good spring.
battles.stakes: Decides whether Minnesota is a win-now team around Justin Jefferson or is still developing its 2024 first-rounder — and effectively decides whether McCarthy has a future with the franchise at all.
battles.moneyNote: This is the rare battle where money argues AGAINST the incumbent: Murray signed a one-year, $1.3M deal in March after Arizona waived him while still owing him roughly $37M, so Minnesota has zero financial incentive to start him. McCarthy carries the draft capital (No. 10 overall, 2024) but the team going out and adding Murray at all is itself a statement of doubt. Neither contract forces the outcome, which is why it is actually open. Reported target for resolution is around Aug. 23, after the joint practices with Baltimore (Aug. 19) and the Aug. 22 exhibition.

battles.why: Minnesota has an opening at safety for the first time in roughly 15 seasons unless Harrison Smith un-retires and plays; Ward and Jackson combined for only 14 starts last year and third-round rookie Jakobe Thomas was drafted into the vacancy.
battles.stakes: Replaces the longest-tenured leadership voice in the secondary and determines how much disguise and post-snap rotation Brian Flores can still run.
battles.moneyNote: No large guarantee anchors this spot. Thomas's third-round capital gives him a runway but not a lock; Ward and Jackson are both on cheap late-round/low-cost deals, so nothing financial decides it. Smith's status is the wild card — if he returns, the competition collapses instantly.

battles.why: The Vikings lost both starting interior linemen this offseason and spent a third-round pick on Orange, who is expected to challenge Rodriguez directly at nose.
battles.stakes: Sets whether Flores can keep playing light boxes and blitz freely, or whether the run defense forces him into more base looks.
battles.moneyNote: Third-round capital on Orange is meaningful but not decisive at DT; Rodriguez is a cheap late-round holdover with no guarantee protecting him. This is a snap-count battle more than a roster-spot battle — both make the team.

battles.why: Minnesota passed on the top free-agent centers and didn't draft one until the seventh round, and O'Connell has said publicly he believes Brandel can handle the snaps, protection and line calls after filling in there last season.
battles.stakes: The pivot in a wide-zone offense with a possibly mobile QB; a bad answer here undermines an otherwise strong line of Fries and Jackson at guard.
battles.moneyNote: The lack of investment IS the tell: no free-agent center signed, a seventh-round pick (Gerhardt) as the only draft addition, plus an explicit coach endorsement of Brandel. Gerhardt and Jurgens are competing for the backup job, not the starting one. Treat 'center battle' headlines skeptically. Separately, Will Fries is entering a pivotal year with a cap hit that jumps after this season — the real OL decision is 2027, not camp.

battles.why: A 36-year-old veteran against a young challenger, with reporting suggesting the tiebreaker is who holds better for Will Reichard.
battles.stakes: Low ceiling either way, but the holder half of the job matters more than the punting half given Reichard's value.
battles.moneyNote: No guaranteed money on either side — specialist camp battles are among the few that money genuinely does not decide. Caveat: some of the punting-competition reporting I found may be recycled from the prior camp cycle, so verify the current names before publishing. Kicker is NOT a battle — Reichard is a first-team All-Pro with no camp competition.

MIN.biggestUnknown: The quarterback. Not just who starts Week 1, but whether J.J. McCarthy — the No. 10 overall pick in 2024 — is the Vikings' future at all. A Murray win doesn't just set a lineup; it triggers trade speculation on McCarthy and reframes the entire roster as win-now. Everything else on this roster is a snap-share question. This one is an identity question.
MIN.campOpens: Rookies reported July 26, 2026; veterans report July 28 at the TCO Performance Center in Eagan. Practices reported to run Aug. 1–20, with joint practices against Baltimore beginning Aug. 19 and a preseason game Aug. 22.
MIN.notes:
Method caveat first: I burned the search budget and nearly every target page (ESPN, Star Tribune, Daily Norseman, PurplePTSD, Vikings.com, SI) returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch, so this is built from search-result summaries of those outlets rather than full article reads. Names and roles are consistent across multiple sources, but verify exact spellings and any single-source claim before it goes to print.

Things a data-driven writer would want:

1) The QB battle inverts the usual money heuristic. Normally you'd say 'follow the guarantees' and stop. Here the veteran is on $1.3M and the kid has the draft capital, so the usual tiebreaker points at McCarthy while the reporting points at Murray. That contradiction is the story. The Cardinals eating ~$37M to release Murray is also a data point about how the last team valued him.

2) Running back is a usage question dressed as a battle. Aaron Jones Sr. vs. Jordan Mason is being framed as a competition; both are making the team and both will play. The interesting number is Mason's fit in wide zone — roughly 3.5 yards after contact per carry — which argues he earns more than a backup share regardless of who is announced as 'the starter.' I'd treat 'RB1' headlines as media-manufactured and write about the touch split instead.

3) Caleb Banks (2026 first-round pick) is reported as expected to win a starting defensive end job IF his broken left foot is fully healed. That is draft capital plus organizational intent, so it is not a real competition — it is a health watch. The honest angle is the injury timeline, not a depth-chart fight.

4) Cornerback appears largely set: Isaiah Rodgers plus an addition from Pittsburgh expected to start opposite him, with Byron Murphy Jr., Dwight McGlothern Jr. and Zemaiah Vaughn behind. I could not confirm the Pittsburgh addition's first name from the summaries I could access — confirm before naming him.

5) Real roster-bubble stories worth chasing that are not starting battles: Ivan Pace's roster security has been openly questioned, and the back-end WR spots (Dillon Bell, who generated minicamp buzz, and UDFA Dontae Fleming) are genuinely open. Those are cut-day stories, not depth-chart stories.

6) The structural story nobody has framed well: Minnesota lost Jonathan Greenard and BOTH starting interior defensive linemen. Dallas Turner (2024 first-rounder, No. 17) stepping into a full-time role is not a battle — it's an assignment. The unsettled part is entirely interior.

battles.why: Adams is the incumbent (694 snaps, 11 starts at RG last year) but the Cardinals spent a 2026 second-round pick on Bisontis, and Adams' offseason arrest on gun charges in Canada clouded his standing.
battles.stakes: The last unsettled spot on an offensive line that has to protect a stopgap QB and open lanes for the No. 3 overall pick, in Mike LaFleur's first year running the offense.
battles.moneyNote: Bisontis is a 2026 second-round pick on a fully guaranteed rookie deal; Adams is a 2024 third-rounder in year three with no guarantees left worth protecting. Second-round capital plus an off-field legal issue on the incumbent tilts this toward the rookie, but Adams did enter camp taking first-team work.

battles.why: Jalen Thompson left in free agency and the job is genuinely vacant; Wingard was signed from Jacksonville and opened camp with the ones, while Taylor-Demerson was the presumed heir.
battles.stakes: Determines whether Arizona can play Baker as a true free defender or has to cover for a second safety, in a secondary otherwise built on young draft picks.
