battles.moneyNote: Wingard signed as a modest veteran free agent with little to no guaranteed money past 2026; Taylor-Demerson is a 2024 fourth-rounder. Neither side has money or capital that decides this — one of the few battles on the roster where the depth chart really is being written in camp.

battles.why: Will Johnson (boundary) and Garrett Williams (slot) are locked in, but the third corner spot has four credible bodies and no incumbent.
battles.stakes: Arizona plays a lot of nickel and dime; the third corner is effectively a starter, and Melton and Burke are the young pieces the defense's future depends on.
battles.moneyNote: Burke led the team in interceptions (3) and passes defensed (11) as a rookie, which is the strongest on-field claim; Melton is a 2024 second-rounder, so mid-round draft capital exists on both sides and cancels out. Murphy-Bunting is the veteran floor, not the favorite.

battles.position: RB rotation behind Jeremiyah Love (and the RB4 roster spot)
battles.why: Arizona took Love third overall, signed Allgeier in free agency, and reworked Conner's deal — four backs, and realistically three roster spots plus one meaningful complementary role.
battles.stakes: Whether the offense has a clear identity behind a rebuilt line, and whether a 2024 third-round back gets cut two years in.
battles.moneyNote: Love is the No. 3 overall pick — a top-five back on a fully guaranteed rookie contract does not lose touches in August, so the 'who starts' framing is settled. What is genuinely open is Benson's roster spot: a 2024 third-rounder coming off a knee injury with no remaining guarantees, squeezed by Allgeier's new free agent deal and Conner's reworked contract.

battles.why: Minshew ran the first-team offense on the opening day of camp while Brissett was working back from a contract standoff, which produced a wave of 'competition' stories.
battles.stakes: Post-Kyler Murray, the entire 2026 season rests on whether a bridge quarterback can function in LaFleur's system.
battles.moneyNote: Brissett's reworked 2026 deal pays $15.5M fully guaranteed (max $21M) — a team does not guarantee that in July and then bench the player in August. LaFleur confirmed Brissett works with the starting offense; Minshew is on a ~$5.75M deal and Beck is a rookie. Minshew's day-one first-team reps were a contract-timing artifact, not a competition.

ARI.campOpens: Veterans fully reported July 22, 2026 at State Farm Stadium (Glendale); first practice July 24. Arizona and Carolina were the first two teams to report because they play the Aug. 6 Hall of Fame Game.
ARI.biggestUnknown: Whether the quarterback position is functional at all. The depth chart is settled — Brissett's $15.5M guarantee decided that — but he went 1-11 as a starter in 2025, Kyler Murray was released in March, and the fallback options are Gardner Minshew and rookie Carson Beck. Nothing else on this roster carries that much unresolved variance.
ARI.notes:
Context a data writer should have: this is a regime change, not a normal camp. Jonathan Gannon was fired in January after a dismal 2025; Mike LaFleur is the first-year head coach, and every projected depth chart from before March is stale. Kyler Murray was released in March and signed with Minnesota.

Two battles I judged real but left off the top five: (1) EDGE opposite Josh Sweat — Sweat had a career-best 12 sacks and is locked in on his free agent money, but the second edge spot is open between 2023 second-rounder BJ Ojulari, 2025 third-rounder Jordan Burch, and Baron Browning. Genuine, and probably the defense's biggest swing factor after the secondary. (2) WR4/WR5 — Michael Wilson (first 1,000-yard season), Marvin Harrison Jr., and Kendrick Bourne are set; Brooks, Weaver, Duvernay, and Fehoko are fighting for the back-end spots, largely on special teams value. Genuine but low-stakes.

The most interesting usage note: LaFleur described the receiver plan as Wilson in the Puka Nacua role and Harrison as the Davante Adams — i.e., Harrison is being deployed as a red-zone/release-point specialist rather than the volume alpha. That is a target-share story worth modeling, and it is a bigger deal than any of the listed battles for fantasy or efficiency work.

Method caveat: SI/OnSI, ESPN, Yahoo, and ArizonaSports all returned HTTP 403 to direct fetches, so the detail below comes from search-result summaries of those beat pieces rather than full article text. The battles and contenders are corroborated across multiple outlets; specific quotes and rep counts are second-hand. Hence medium, not high, confidence. I did not find any reporting on a kicker or punter competition.

DAL.campOpens: Veterans and rookies reported to Oxnard, CA on Tue July 28, 2026; opening press conference and first practice Wed July 29; first padded practice Mon Aug 3; Oxnard portion ends Aug 18 before the team returns to Ford Center at The Star in Frisco

battles.why: Repeatedly described by beat coverage as the most questionable room on the roster: Overshown has a serious injury history, Winters was acquired in a trade from San Francisco rather than paid as a lock, and third-round rookie Barham is converting from a college edge/hybrid role into a full-time off-ball job in Christian Parker's new 3-4.
battles.stakes: The green-dot communicator in a first-year scheme installing up to seven new defensive starters — this is the position most likely to determine whether a defense that allowed a league-worst 30 PPG in 2025 actually improves.
battles.moneyNote: No one here has meaningful guaranteed money. Barham is 2026 third-round capital (real but not decisive); Winters arrived by trade on a modest deal; Overshown's leverage is entirely health-dependent.

battles.why: Bland is the only locked starter (and has a nagging foot issue that has cost him games in each of the last two seasons). Revel gets his first healthy NFL offseason in Year 2, Durant was signed in the first week of free agency, and Dallas kept stacking bodies at the position through the draft and into July.
battles.stakes: With Caleb Downs taking slot reps, whoever wins the outside job opposite Bland plays close to every snap; the loser becomes expensive depth on a defense that gets tested deep.
battles.moneyNote: Durant's free-agent deal gives him a floor, and Revel carries 2025 third-round capital, but neither has the kind of guarantee that ends a competition. Kendrick is on a one-year deal and is a genuine cut candidate. Moore is 2026 fourth-round capital — depth, not a mandate.

battles.why: Brian Schottenheimer publicly opened it — 'Tyler's biggest thing is the consistency has not been there,' and 'we're going to make Tyler earn it' — after Dallas cycled through three left tackles in 2025.
battles.stakes: Protecting Dak Prescott's blind side on a line that ranked 19th in pass block win rate in 2025; it is the offense's one soft spot next to Lamb/Pickens.
battles.moneyNote: Guyton is the 2024 first-round pick (No. 29) on a fully guaranteed rookie deal with a fifth-year option decision coming — teams essentially never bench that in camp. Jon Machota (The Athletic) reported Guyton took all the first-team reps through minicamp and remains the 'clear favorite.' Thomas was drafted 204 picks later; Shelton is a developmental 2026 fourth-rounder. The competition is real as motivation, not as an outcome.

battles.why: Javonte Williams is the entrenched starter after a 1,201-yard 2025, but he took 287 touches and faded with a shoulder injury; Dallas has openly said it needs a second back to carry load. Blue is the change-of-pace/receiving option they hope it is, but ball security and pass protection are the open questions.
battles.stakes: Roughly 100-140 touches and the third-down/passing-down role behind a back Dallas cannot afford to run into the ground again.
battles.moneyNote: Nobody in the room has guaranteed money. Blue is 2025 fifth-round capital — enough to earn the reps, not enough to survive a bad camp; at least one national outlet has floated him as a surprise cut.

battles.why: CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, and Jake Ferguson are locked, so the fight is purely for the last skill-position spots. UDFA Michael Trigg has generated real buzz at TE3, and Mingo is fighting for the fifth WR job against 2026 draftee Anthony Smith.
battles.stakes: Special-teams value and injury insurance for the league's most top-heavy skill group; also whether Dallas finally cuts bait on a former Day 2 tight end.
battles.moneyNote: Schoonmaker is 2023 second-round capital, but that capital is now three years old and near the end of its rookie deal — the point at which it stops protecting a player. Mingo cost Dallas a Day 2-ish trade asset, which is the main thing keeping him on the roster. Smith is 2026 late-round capital.

DAL.biggestUnknown: Whether first-year coordinator Christian Parker's 3-4 defense — with as many as seven new starters, a rookie first-rounder at safety, and an unsettled off-ball linebacker room — can be functional by September. Everything else on this roster is a depth question; the defense is a structural one.
DAL.notes: Things a data-driven writer should know: (1) The LT story is the most-written Cowboys camp battle and is probably the least real one — the coach opened it verbally, the rep counts closed it. Beat reporting from minicamp had Guyton taking every first-team snap. Treat 'Schottenheimer opened a competition' as motivational language, not a depth-chart signal. (2) Safety is NOT a battle despite the crowded room: Dallas traded up to No. 11 for Caleb Downs, who was already working the slot in spring, and reworked Malik Hooker's deal (~$6.56M cap hit) in March, which functionally guaranteed Hooker a spot. Jalen Thompson and P.J. Locke were added on top. Any 'safety competition' framing is manufactured. (3) Right guard and center are settled — Tyler Booker (2025 first-rounder, good rookie year) at RG and Cooper Beebe at C. (4) George Pickens signed the franchise tag at $27.3M and committed to full camp participation, so the 'will Pickens hold in' storyline is dead; that is context, not a battle. (5) Kicker is not open — Brandon Aubrey. (6) The Cowboys' 2026 draft went five of seven picks on defense (Downs at 11, edge Malachi Lawrence in Rd 1, LB Jaishawn Barham Rd 3, plus three fourth-rounders including CB Devin Moore and OT Drew Shelton), which tells you where the front office itself thought the roster was unsettled — and it matches where the genuine battles are. (7) Caveat on sourcing: several of the primary pages (dallascowboys.com, SI/OnSI, Blogging The Boys) returned 403 to direct fetch, so specifics below the starter level come from search-result summaries rather than full articles. A couple of roster details (exact backup names at ILB and RB3) should be re-verified against a live depth chart before publication.

LAC.campOpens: Rookies reported July 23, 2026; full squad/first camp practice July 29, 2026 at The Bolt in El Segundo, CA (camp runs through late August)

battles.why: It is the only genuinely open starting job on the roster — Slater and Alt return at tackle, Tyler Biadasz was signed to start at center and Cole Strange at right guard, leaving LG as the one unfilled spot after a heavy OL investment offseason.
battles.stakes: It is the last hole in a line that has to keep Justin Herbert upright in Mike McDaniel's first year running the offense, with both starting tackles coming off season-ending injuries.
battles.moneyNote: Slaughter was the No. 63 pick (2nd round, 2026) — real but not overwhelming draft capital, and he has not played guard since high school after starring at center at Florida. Awosika is a cheap veteran FA signing (11 career starts in Detroit) and Penning is a re-signed swing lineman working with the third team. No one here has guaranteed money large enough to decide it, which is exactly why it is open. Awosika led in the spring; McDaniel said he would not really evaluate it until the pads come on, and Harbaugh in mid-June called the competition "raging on."

battles.position: S2 / deep safety next to Elijah Molden
battles.why: Trading Alohi Gilman last season left no clear-cut deep safety alongside Derwin James and Molden, and the Chargers did not sign a starter-priced replacement.
battles.stakes: Chris O'Leary's defense leans on James playing everywhere; the second safety determines how freely they can move him and how much three-safety nickel they can run.
battles.moneyNote: Nobody in the room has money or capital that settles it. Jefferson is a minimum-level unretired veteran, Mickens a 2025 late-round pick coming off 328 rookie snaps, Genesis Smith a 2026 fourth-rounder. Derwin James signed a multi-year extension in late May, which locks the other safety spot but not this one.

battles.position: EDGE4 / rotational edge behind Mack, Tuipulotu, Mesidor
battles.why: Odafe Oweh left in free agency and the Chargers replaced him at the top with a first-rounder, leaving the fourth spot and the associated roster/snap allocation unresolved.
battles.stakes: Determines how much Mack (aging) and Tuipulotu can be rested, and whether an aging veteran holds a roster spot over a young rusher.
battles.moneyNote: Akheem Mesidor, the No. 22 overall pick in 2026, is not in this competition — his first-round capital already guarantees him rotational snaps regardless of camp. The actual battle is behind him: Dupree is a low-cost veteran and a named cut candidate, Kennard a 2025 Day 3 pick, Tucker an undrafted rookie. Low money all around means this one really gets decided on the field.

battles.why: The top three receivers are set, but the back end of the room is unsettled and the return job was openly rotated in minicamp among Hampton, Mitchell, Vidal, Ross and Jackson.
battles.stakes: McDaniel's scheme needs more than three usable receivers, and return duty is often the tiebreaker for the last one or two WR/RB roster spots.
battles.moneyNote: Brenen Thompson is a 2026 fourth-rounder with the fastest 40 at the Combine, which gives him a leg up but not a lock; Derius Davis is a returner-first incumbent with no guaranteed money protecting him. Keaton Mitchell is a cheap FA add brought in to replace Najee Harris's early-down role and is competing with tendered ERFA Kimani Vidal (643 rush yards in 2025) for the RB2 job behind Omarion Hampton.

battles.why: Johnston's drops and the emergence of second-year Tre' Harris generate an annual "is he losing the job" storyline.
battles.stakes: Very little in camp — the real question is 2027, when the option money comes due.
battles.moneyNote: This is the decisive fact: the Chargers exercised Johnston's fifth-year option in late April 2026, paying him $4.5M in 2026 and fully guaranteeing $18M for 2027. A team does not guarantee $18M to a player it intends to demote in August. He led the team in touchdowns in each of the last two seasons and set a career high with 735 yards in 14 games. Harris will take snaps and may out-produce him, but the starting designation is not in play.

LAC.biggestUnknown: Whether the completely rebuilt offensive interior holds up in Mike McDaniel's brand-new offense — the left guard spot is unfilled, Biadasz and Strange are first-year additions at center and right guard, and both bookends (Rashawn Slater, torn patellar tendon in last year's camp; Joe Alt, ankle) are returning from season-ending injuries. Everything about the 2026 Chargers offense is downstream of that.
LAC.notes: Context a data-driven writer should have: (1) This is year three of Harbaugh, and he fired OC Greg Roman and hired Mike McDaniel — a scheme change that makes 2025 usage and efficiency data a poor predictor of 2026 roles, especially for the receivers and for Ladd McConkey. (2) The linebacker room is deep enough that it did not make my top five, but it is worth watching: Daiyan Henley and Denzel Perryman are described by beat coverage as the defined starters, so I would call the LB2 job likely-settled — yet Junior Colson (2024 third-rounder, poor rookie year, missed 2025 with a shoulder injury) is simultaneously a breakout candidate and a 53-man-roster cut candidate, with Troy Dye the favorite for the first rotational role and Marlowe Wax/Del'Shawn Phillips behind. That is a roster-spot battle, not a starting battle. (3) Henley is the team's most important extension candidate entering camp — a contract story, not a competition. (4) No kicker competition surfaced in any reporting; treat kicker as settled. (5) The Chargers drafted eight players and signed 18 UDFAs, four of the eight picks being offensive linemen — the volume of OL bodies (17 in the room) is itself the story, and it means the LG loser probably still makes the roster. (6) Beware aggregator lists that inflate WR3 and \"starting RB\" into battles; Johnston's option and Omarion Hampton's first-round status make both non-competitions.

CLE.notes:
Things a data-driven writer should know:

1) The most important framing on the QB battle is counterintuitive. Watson's guarantee is usually cited as the reason he plays — but 2026 is the last year of that deal and the money is owed regardless of snaps. It is pure sunk cost with no forward incentive, which is precisely why this competition is genuinely open where it was not in 2023-24. A first-year head coach in Monken adds to that.

2) Sanders' 2025 rookie sample is the case against him, not for him: 3-4 as a starter, roughly 1,400 yards, 7 TD, 10 INT after taking over midseason from Dillon Gabriel. That is a ~4.5% interception rate territory line. Anyone writing "Sanders is clearly better" is arguing from vibes, not production. The honest read is two unproven options.

3) The 2026 draft class quietly pre-decided several "battles." First-rounders K.C. Concepcion (WR) and Spencer Fano (OT), second-rounders Denzel Boston (WR, No. 39) and Emmanuel McNeil-Warren (S) are all playing. Any list that includes those spots as camp competitions is padding.

4) The secondary is a health story, not a competition story. Denzel Ward, Grant Delpit and McNeil-Warren all missed on-field work in OTAs/minicamp with injuries. Ward-Tyson Campbell is set at corner; CB3 behind them (Myles Bryant, Myles Harden, newly signed Damarri Mathis) is genuinely thin and worth a look, but it is a depth problem more than a battle. Cleveland waived CB Dom Jones on a failed physical.

5) One real battle I left out for space: swing tackle, Dawand Jones vs. rookie Austin Barber. Jones has bounced between both tackle spots across three seasons without ever staying healthy enough to lock either down. Low money, low capital, genuinely open — worth a mention if you want a sixth.

6) Njoku's departure is the cleanest quantitative story on this roster. Fannin already led the team in receptions as a rookie (72) with Njoku still there; the vacated target share has no established second tight end to absorb it, which points to concentration rather than a split.

7) Watch the interior OL alignment reporting rather than the "competition" framing. The five bodies are chosen by contract; the interesting question is whether Elgton Jenkins plays center (his Packers role) and where Zion Johnson lands after Los Angeles took him 17th overall in 2022.

battles.why: Taylor Decker was released this offseason and Penei Sewell slid to left tackle, vacating right tackle entirely; the Lions then spent the No. 17 pick on Miller and signed Borom in free agency the same spring.
battles.stakes: The only starting spot on the line in front of Jared Goff with no incumbent, being sorted under a first-year offensive coordinator (Drew Petzing) with no joint practices to stress-test it.
battles.moneyNote: Real competition in July, but the thumb is on the scale. Miller is the No. 17 overall pick, signed, and the team released Decker to make this configuration possible. Borom's 1-year, $5M deal (~$4.90M guaranteed) is swing-tackle insurance pricing - enough to make him a credible Week 1 answer if Miller stumbles, not enough to hold the job all season against first-round capital. Expect Borom to win reps and Miller to win the season.

battles.why: Mahogany is the incumbent, but Detroit deliberately stacked the room in free agency because his 2025 play didn't settle the spot; beat coverage frames it as him needing to show real improvement to hold off two additions.
battles.stakes: Combined with the RT opening, Detroit could start two brand-new offensive line pieces in front of a 31-year-old Goff behind a brand-new play-caller.
battles.moneyNote: The cleanest genuinely open job on the roster, because nobody is financially or positionally protected: Mahogany is a 2024 sixth-round pick (no capital shield), Bartch and Scruggs are both journeyman-priced veterans. One wrinkle that matters: Bartch sat out the entire offseason program rehabbing an injury, so he enters behind on reps despite being seen as the top challenger. Scruggs' three-position interior versatility may make him more valuable as a swing backup than as a starter.

battles.position: Third linebacker / weakside LB (Alex Anzalone's vacated role)
battles.why: Anzalone signed with Tampa Bay, leaving Jack Campbell (All-Pro in 2025) and Derrick Barnes (SAM) as the only established linebackers; Detroit drafted Rolder in the fourth round specifically as the replacement archetype.
battles.stakes: Detroit led the NFL in base-defense (three-linebacker) snaps in 2025 and Sheppard has signaled a move toward nickel and hybrid defenders in year two - so this decides whether LB3 is a 60% starter or a 30% situational player.
battles.moneyNote: No money or capital decides this. Rodriguez has the early edge purely on four years of familiarity with Sheppard's system, not on contract. Rolder is a Day 3 pick, exactly the range where rookies do lose camp battles. Honest read: the job may shrink before it is won - if Sheppard goes nickel-heavy, the winner plays materially fewer snaps than Anzalone did.

battles.why: Kalif Raymond's departure opened the slot/return utility role, and Detroit added four UFL receivers to the 90-man to compete for the back of the room.
battles.stakes: Low individually, real cumulatively - these spots are decided as much by Dave Fipp's special teams needs as by receiving ability, and they determine whether Detroit can carry an extra body elsewhere.
battles.moneyNote: Important framing correction: the WR3 job is NOT open, whatever gets written. Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams (back-to-back 1,000-yard seasons) are locked at 1 and 2, and Isaac TeSlaa took hold of WR3 late in his rookie year with six touchdowns. Dortch was signed with prior familiarity in Petzing's scheme, making him the favorite for the Raymond role. Anyone selling a 'Lions WR3 battle' is manufacturing it.

DET.biggestUnknown: The secondary. Detroit lost its 2024 first-round corner (Terrion Arnold) to a felony arrest and release on June 29 with no replacement plan, opens camp with All-Pro safety Kerby Joseph and star nickel Brian Branch (Achilles) both on PUP, and its one settled outside corner, D.J. Reed, is coming off an injury-shortened season and has not been tested with pads on. Every other battle on this roster is known, healthy candidates competing under normal conditions. This one is a hole with a timeline nobody can give you, landing exactly as Kelvin Sheppard tries to install a more nickel-heavy, matchup-driven scheme that requires the defensive backs he doesn't currently have on the field.
DET.notes: Things a data-driven writer should grab: (1) Detroit led the entire NFL in base-defense snaps in 2025 - that number should crater in 2026 by Sheppard's own stated design, which makes "starting LB3" a misleading label and makes nickel snap share the real stat to track. (2) New OC Drew Petzing is calling plays and the Lions are doing zero joint practices, so preseason snap counts on the OL competitions carry more signal than usual. (3) Two of five OL starting spots turned over in one offseason (Decker released, Sewell moved to LT) - pressure-rate-allowed by side is the story, not raw sack totals. (4) Jahmyr Gibbs is expected to expand into a fuller RB1 workload with Isiah Pacheco signed to replace David Montgomery; that touch redistribution is a bigger efficiency/fantasy story than any Lions position battle. (5) Jack Campbell made All-Pro in 2025 and is the undisputed center of the defense - the one stable pillar to write around. (6) Detroit's 2026 class: Blake Miller (R1, OT), Derrick Moore (R2, EDGE), Jimmy Rolder (R4, LB), Keith Abney II (R5, CB), Kendrick Law (R5, WR), Skyler Gill-Howard (R6, DT), Tyre West (R7, DL) - three of seven picks land directly in the battles above. (7) The framing question ESPN and others are asking is whether the Super Bowl window has closed; every one of these battles gets read through that lens. Caveat on confidence: several primary sources (detroitlions.com, Detroit News, ESPN, SI/OnSI) returned 403 to direct fetch, so contract figures and battle framings come from search-index summaries of those articles rather than full text. The Ya-Sin contract number in particular was reported two different ways ($4M/1yr vs $3.2M/1yr, ~$2.64M guaranteed) - verify before printing an exact figure.

BAL.campOpens: Rookies, QBs and injured veterans reported July 24; veterans report July 28, 2026. First public practice July 29 at the Under Armour Performance Center in Owings Mills; camp runs through Aug. 17.

battles.why: Three-time Pro Bowler Tyler Linderbaum left for the Raiders in free agency and Baltimore did not replace him until signing Pocic 12 days before the first practice, leaving a genuinely open starting job with a health caveat.
battles.stakes: The pivot in front of Lamar Jackson in Declan Doyle's brand-new offense; a bad answer here undercuts the whole scheme installation and the interior line rebuild around John Simpson and rookie Vega Ioane.
battles.moneyNote: Pocic is on a 1-year, $3M deal with $1.5M in incentives — nowhere near enough guaranteed money to hand him the job, and he was only medically cleared from a Dec. 7 torn left Achilles shortly before camp. He has 97 career starts; of Pinter, Gwyn and Bullock only Pinter has ever started an NFL game (never in Week 1, never more than three in a season). Pocic is the clear favorite on résumé, not on money.

battles.why: Kyle Van Noy and Dre'Mont Jones are gone and Baltimore finished near the bottom of the league in sacks in 2025; Hendrickson locks one side, and the other starting spot plus the rotation behind it is unresolved.
battles.stakes: Whether Jesse Minter's first Ravens defense can generate pressure without blitzing — the single biggest reason Baltimore spent $112M on Hendrickson.
battles.moneyNote: Hendrickson (4 years, $112M, $28M AAV) is untouchable — he is not part of any competition. The competition itself is genuinely open because the draft capital is split: Zion Young was the 2026 second-rounder at No. 45 and Mike Green was a 2025 second-rounder, so neither can be cut and both will be force-fed snaps. Robinson (4.5 sacks on 451 snaps in 2025) is the proven-but-cheap incumbent. Expect a rotation rather than a clean winner.

battles.why: Baltimore signed no veteran receiver this offseason and instead drafted two, so everything behind Zay Flowers and Rashod Bateman is up for grabs in a new offensive system.
battles.stakes: Jackson's third and fourth options in Doyle's offense, and whether the Ravens' decision to solve receiver purely through the draft actually works.
battles.moneyNote: Flowers (2023 first-rounder) and Bateman (signed a multi-year extension in 2025) are locked starters and are not competing. Draft capital tilts the back end: Ja'Kobi Lane went in Round 3 (No. 80) and Elijah Sarratt in Round 4 (No. 115), which makes both very likely to make the 53 regardless of camp. The genuinely at-risk players are Wester and Wade. Walker, entering year three, is the incumbent favorite for WR3 but has no contractual protection.

battles.position: CB depth / rotation behind the top three
battles.why: With Marlon Humphrey reportedly sliding inside to nickel and Nate Wiggins and Chidobe Awuzie handling the outside, the CB4-CB6 jobs and the dime package are open.
battles.stakes: Depth insurance for a secondary that has to hold up in a new defensive scheme; Baltimore's 2025 coverage was a documented weakness.
battles.moneyNote: Only the depth spots are live. Humphrey's role is decided by money, not performance — he carries a reported $26.3M 2026 cap hit despite a poor 2025 coverage season, so he plays somewhere regardless. Wiggins (2024 first-rounder) is a lock. Rookie Chandler Rivers (Duke) has mid-round draft capital that gives him an edge for a roster spot over the veteran journeymen.

battles.why: Pro Bowl punter Jordan Stout signed with the Giants, so the job is technically open and the Ravens are running a two-man camp competition.
battles.stakes: Field position for a team that plays close AFC North games — but the outcome is not really in doubt.
battles.moneyNote: Eckley was a sixth-round pick and the first punter off the board in the 2026 draft. Teams essentially never spend a draft pick on a specialist and then lose the job to an unheralded camp body. Treat this as Eckley's job with a token competition attached.

BAL.biggestUnknown: The starting center. Baltimore let a three-time Pro Bowl center walk, went most of the offseason without a real answer, and then patched it with a 1-year, $3M veteran who was medically cleared from a torn Achilles days before camp. Every other unsettled spot on this roster is a rotation or depth question; this one is a Week 1 starting job in front of Lamar Jackson in a first-year offensive scheme, with no fallback who has ever started a season opener.
BAL.notes: Context a data-driven writer should have: (1) Both coordinators are new — Declan Doyle on offense, Jesse Minter on defense — so early-camp "battles" are partly scheme-fit sorting, and depth-chart reporting from June is unusually unreliable. (2) The most consequential variable on this roster is not a competition at all: Nnamdi Madubuike has not played since Week 2 of 2025 after neck surgery, and the team's own preview lists his return as a top question. His health swings the defense more than any camp battle. (3) Baltimore's offseason was pass-rush-first: they rescinded a Maxx Crosby trade over a failed physical and pivoted to Hendrickson at 4 years/$112M. (4) They made 11 picks in the 2026 draft, including G Vega Ioane at No. 14 overall — Ioane is a starter by draft capital, so do not treat guard as a battle. (5) Kicker is settled: Tyler Loop returns after an 88.2% rookie FG season, despite the 44-yard miss in Pittsburgh that ended 2025. (6) Safety is settled: Kyle Hamilton and Malaki Starks. Be careful with aggregators here — several summaries I encountered still described Starks as a "first-round rookie" and Derrick Henry as a new "addition," which is recycled 2024-25 copy. (7) Beware any list that calls RB a battle; only the complementary role behind Henry (Justice Hill vs. Rasheen Ali) is live, and it is low-stakes.

GB.campOpens: Rookies and injured players reported Mon July 27, 2026; veterans follow July 28. First full practice Wed July 29, 10:30 a.m. at Ray Nitschke Field. Camp runs July 29 - Aug 26.

battles.why: Valentine started 11 games there in 2025 and was the secondary's weak link — roughly 60% completion rate allowed on ~780 snaps and a passer rating against over 120 — so the Packers attacked the spot twice this offseason, signing St-Juste and spending their top pick on Cisse.
battles.stakes: Nixon is locked in on one side; the other boundary corner is the most exploitable starting job on a defense installing Jonathan Gannon's scheme. If none of the three separates, teams will target it all year.
battles.moneyNote: Cisse was Green Bay's FIRST pick of the 2026 draft (2nd round, No. 52 overall — the Packers had no 1st-rounder after the Micah Parsons trade), which is the single biggest thumb on the scale here; draft capital says he ends up the starter even if he doesn't win it in August. St-Juste signed a fresh veteran free-agent deal in March off a career year as PFF's highest-graded zone corner with the Chargers. Valentine is the cheap incumbent (2023 7th-rounder) with no guaranteed money protecting him — the classic profile of a starter who loses his job. Exact guarantee figures for St-Juste were not verifiable in available reporting.

battles.why: Belton, the 2025 second-round pick, was bad as a rookie — seven starts in 14 games and a 49.7 PFF grade that ranked 72nd of 81 qualifying guards — and the Packers drafted Burton in the fifth round to push him. Beat reporting has both taking first-team reps entering camp.
battles.stakes: This is the interior protection in front of Jordan Love and the one spot on an otherwise settled offensive line that can actively cost the offense games.
battles.moneyNote: Belton has the draft capital (2025 Rd 2) and a second-round rookie contract, which normally decides these outright — a Round 2 pick in Year 2 almost never loses to a Round 5 rookie. What makes this genuinely open rather than settled is that the coaching staff is reportedly splitting first-team reps, which is a real signal, not a media invention. Lean Belton, but treat it as live.

battles.position: EDGE (starter opposite Lukas Van Ness for the first 4-5 games)
battles.why: Micah Parsons is slated to open the season on PUP after a torn ACL late in 2025, which sidelines him at least the first four games (reporting suggests five). Van Ness holds one side; the other starting job is unclaimed.
battles.stakes: Green Bay's defensive identity is the pass rush. A month of games without Parsons against an early schedule is where the season can get away from them before he's back.
battles.moneyNote: No money or draft capital resolves this — Cox, Sorrell and Oliver are all late-round/cheap, and Dennis-Sutton is a 4th-rounder (No. 120). The job is genuinely up for grabs precisely because nobody in the group has been paid. Caveat: it is a temporary job with a hard expiration date when Parsons is activated, which caps how much the winner actually matters.

battles.why: Gannon is installing a three-man base front and the roster has essentially no incumbent nose tackle — Gannon said publicly in March the D-line needed more size. Riley, the only veteran option, tore an Achilles and is questionable for the opener.
battles.stakes: If nobody wins it, the base front gets displaced against the run and the Packers are forced into nickel personnel as their default, which is a scheme problem, not a depth problem.
battles.moneyNote: McClellan is the 2026 third-round pick, so he has the capital edge over Stackhouse (2025, minimum-level deal). Javon Hargrave's two-year, $23M deal ($13M in 2026) is real guaranteed money but he's a penetrating 3-tech, not the answer at true nose — don't let his signing be read as settling this spot.

battles.position: WR4 / WR5 and the return job
battles.why: The Packers traded Dontayvion Wicks to Philadelphia and let Romeo Doubs walk, which several outlets framed as opening 'the most compelling positional battle on the roster.' It isn't. The top three are locked and the real fight is for snaps 4 through 6.
battles.stakes: Low. Whoever wins WR5 gets special teams work and injury insurance. The actual question in this room is whether Savion Williams becomes a real route-runner, and that is a development question, not a competition.
battles.moneyNote: Christian Watson and Jayden Reed both signed extensions this offseason — that is guaranteed money that ends any debate about their roles. Matthew Golden was the 2025 first-round pick. Savion Williams (2025 Rd 3) is the presumed WR4 and the team has signaled publicly it likes him there. Skyy Moore was signed as a cheap returner, not as a threat to anyone's starting job. Four of the top five spots are decided by money or draft capital before a single practice.

GB.biggestUnknown: Whether the front seven can function for the first month without Micah Parsons — he opens on PUP (out at least four games, reportedly five) while Gannon simultaneously installs a 3-4 base the roster has no true nose tackle for. The starting EDGE opposite an unproven Lukas Van Ness and the starting nose tackle are both genuinely vacant at the same time, on the same unit, in a new scheme.
GB.notes:
Two more "battles" you'll see written up that you should discount, plus one real one that's being under-covered:

KICKER — NOT A BATTLE, resolved in May. Green Bay drafted Trey Smack (Florida) in the 6th round, the only kicker taken in the 2026 draft, then released Brandon McManus 13 days later. Zone Coverage's headline was literally "Green Bay's Kicking Competition Is Over Before It Began." Smack is the kicker barring a disastrous August. Context if you want the narrative: McManus missed three kicks in the wild-card loss at Chicago, leaving 7 points off the board in a 4-point defeat, after struggling back from a quad injury to his kicking leg. Label this likely-settled, decided by draft capital plus the veteran's release.

RB2 — genuinely open, lower stakes than the coverage implies. Emanuel Wilson (254 touches over two seasons) left for Seattle. The candidates are MarShawn Lloyd — highest ceiling in the room, 2024 third-round pick, but has barely played due to recurring hamstring issues — and Chris Brooks, re-signed on a two-year deal and profiling as an RB3. Josh Jacobs is a bell-cow, so the winner's snap share is small unless Jacobs misses time. Reporting also references unresolved questions around Jacobs' contract structure and an offseason issue; I could not verify the specifics and would not run with it without a second source.

TE — worth checking before you publish. Tucker Kraft went down in 2025 (Achilles per most accounts) and his availability for Week 1 is the biggest offensive variable on the roster. Luke Musgrave and Josh Whyle were the fallback and did not produce. ESPN ran a camp preview specifically headlined on Parsons' and Kraft's return timelines that I could not open — that's your first call.

ROSTER CONTEXT worth a line in any piece: the Packers have no 2026 or 2027 first-round pick (traded to Dallas for Parsons), so Brandon Cisse at No. 52 is functionally their first-rounder. That's why the CB2 job tilts toward him regardless of how camp looks. Other offseason adds: Javon Hargrave (2 yr / $23M, $13M in 2026) signed within an hour of his release by Minnesota, LB Zaire Franklin acquired from Indianapolis for Colby Wooden, and WR/returner Skyy Moore.

The battle structure and contenders are corroborated across multiple independent sources and I'm confident in them.
